Friendly fraud prevention comes down to three jobs you can do in code: log the right checkout data, block risky payments before they settle, and automate your response when a dispute still lands. Get the first one wrong and you can't win the dispute later, no matter how good your case is.

According to recent reports, in this tutorial, we'll build each piece in Node.js in a way that works with any payment service provider (PSP). Your code owns the data and the logic, and a thin adapter talks to Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com or whoever processes your payments.

It has been revealed that friendly fraud happens when a customer makes a real purchase, then disputes it with their card issuer. They might claim they didn't authorize it, that it never arrived, or that they canceled. Sometimes it's honest confusion. A spouse used the saved card, or the charge highlighted up under a name they didn't recognize. Sometimes it's a free refund with extra steps.

Either way, the money leaves your account. A dispute (also called a chargeback) reverses the payment, and your processor charges a dispute fee on top. Lose too many, and the card networks put your account into a monitoring program with higher fees.

It's also common. Visa puts friendly fraud at around 20% of fraudulent disputes globally, and up to 30% for high-volume online merchants. Mastercard goes further: it notes first-party fraud makes up 75% of the fraud online businesses experience.

Sources indicate that so why is this your problem and not finance's? Because the evidence that wins these disputes is created at checkout, by your code. If your app never stored the customer's IP address, device ID or login history, nobody can produce it three months later when the dispute arrives.

Friendly fraud can be stopped at four points, and each one is a different piece of code:.

It has been revealed that most guides only cover stages 1 and 4. The rest of this tutorial walks through all four.

Log four things on every order: the customer's IP address, a device ID, their account ID and the shipping address. Those are the data elements Visa's Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE3.0) rules check when you fight an "unauthorized" fraud dispute.

According to recent reports, here's how CE3.0 works. You win the dispute if you can show two earlier, undisputed purchases on the same card, made 120 to 365 days before the disputed one. All three purchases must share at least two data elements, and one of them must be the IP address or device ID. In plain terms: same card, same person, same device, and they never complained before.

Most PSPs support CE3.0, including Stripe, Adyen, Checkout.com and Airwallex. But none of them can submit data you never captured. And because the window reaches back a full year, you need to keep these logs for at least 13 months (Mastercard's rule, below).

According to recent reports, mastercard has its own version, called First-Party Trust, for disputes filed under reason code 4837 (no cardholder authorization). It asks for one data point from each of three categories: a device factor (IP address, device ID or fingerprint), a delivery factor (shipping address, email or phone) and a different identity factor (such as account login ID or billing address). On the dispute route, Mastercard calls a lookup service that you host, with named fields such as deviceIpAddress, orderDeviceId, orderEmail and userIdName. That service has to answer in about 2.5 seconds on average and search 13 months of sales data.

First-Party Trust is live in the US. Per Mastercard's October 2026 announcement, it reaches Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa from October 2026 and the rest of Europe from July 2027. If you sell into Europe, the logging work is due now.

Two storage rules save you pain later:.

The good news: one evidence table serves both networks. Capture the data once, then keep the eligibility checks for Visa and Mastercard separate.

Start with a table that stores this data per order, separate from your PSP:.

Sources indicate that then capture it in your checkout route. If your app sits behind a proxy or CDN, set Express's trust proxy so req.ip returns the customer's address, not your load balancer's:.

The psp object is your adapter: one small module per provider that maps its API to the same shape. Swap providers, and this route doesn't change.

In a recent development, for digital products and SaaS, log usage too. Login timestamps, downloads and feature activity prove the customer used what they paid for, which beats "I never received it" claims.

The cheapest dispute is the one that never happens. Three checkout changes do most of the work: 3D Secure on risky payments, a billing descriptor customers recognize, and a few rules that stop obvious abuse.

Use 3D Secure where risk is higher. 3D Secure (3DS) asks the cardholder to confirm the payment with their bank, often through an app prompt. For authenticated payments, liability for fraud disputes generally shifts from you to the card issuer. Every major PSP supports it, and most let you request it per payment instead of forcing it on everyone. Forcing it everywhere adds friction and costs conversions, so trigger it on risk signals.

According to recent reports, make your billing descriptor obvious. The descriptor is the text on the customer's card statement. If it reads PMT*SRV 8812 instead of your product name, expect "I don't recognize this charge" disputes. Use the brand name customers know, and add a support URL or phone number where your PSP allows it. If you sell several products, use a dynamic descriptor that names each one.

Add a risk check before you charge. Most PSPs include a rules engine, but a small check in your own code keeps the logic portable:.

According to recent reports, store the signals array with the order. If a dispute arrives later, you'll know whether the payment looked risky at the time, which helps you decide whether to fight it or accept it.

Industry observers note that keep the rules few and specific. A rule that blocks 5% of good customers to stop 1% of bad ones costs more than the disputes it prevents.

Yes, if you ship physical goods. The window between a successful payment and the moment an order ships is the cheapest place to stop friendly fraud: nothing has left the warehouse, so canceling costs you nothing but the sale. Most fraud tools decide at checkout and never look again.

Industry observers note that the pattern is a fulfillment gate. Instead of sending every paid order straight to your warehouse or 3PL, route it through a decision step first:.

The verify path does two jobs. Legitimate buyers confirm and their order ships. Buyers planning to dispute see that the store is watching, and a confirmed verification becomes evidence if they dispute anyway.

The hard part is screenOrder. Your own data only demonstrates how a customer behaved with you. A buyer who has filed "item not received" disputes at 10 other stores looks brand new on their first order with yours. That's why post-purchase screening works best on shared data across many merchants.

It has been revealed that chargeflow Prevent is one example of this kind of friendly fraud prevention. It scores each order after checkout and before fulfillment, links device, IP, email and payment behavior across a network of 20,000+ merchants, and returns approve, verify or cancel. Today it runs as a Shopify app, with no checkout changes. A public Prevent API isn't available yet, so on other stacks you'd build the gate above with your own rules and data.

Build an order lookup endpoint. When a cardholder taps "I don't recognize this" in their banking app, the issuer can now ask the merchant for order details before a dispute is filed. Visa does this through Verifi Order Insight, and Mastercard through Ethoca Consumer Clarity. Show the customer a receipt with your logo, the items and the delivery date, and many disputes are never filed.

One endpoint can serve both networks, plus Mastercard's First-Party Trust dispute route. Mastercard's published service levels for this kind of lookup are strict:.

Sources indicate that the tricky part is matching. Issuers often send partial data, so match on whatever arrives: acquirer reference number (ARN), authorization code, date, amount, currency, and card BIN plus last four digits.

Recent findings suggest that on top of lookups, Visa and many PSPs offer rules-based auto-refunds. Verifi's Rapid Dispute Resolution (RDR) and Visa Resolve refund pre-disputes that match rules you set, such as "refund anything under $25". You don't write code for these, but you do pick the thresholds, so treat them like the REFUND_THRESHOLD below.

If you sell subscriptions, many friendly fraud disputes aren't about stolen cards at all. The customer forgot about a renewal, couldn't find the cancel button, or thinks they canceled. Each of these has a code fix.

Here's a daily job that sends renewal reminders and records that each one went out:.

In a recent development, that evidenceLog row matters. When a customer later claims they never knew about the renewal, you can show the exact date you told them.

Recent findings suggest that automate two things: refunding payments that get flagged before they become chargebacks, and building evidence packets for the ones you fight. Both run off webhooks, and both have hard deadlines that humans miss.

According to recent reports, card networks can warn you before a dispute is filed. Visa runs this through Verifi and Mastercard through Ethoca, and many PSPs pass these alerts or their own early fraud warnings to you by webhook. Refunding at this stage costs you the sale, but you skip the dispute fee and the dispute doesn't count against your ratio.

The threshold is a business call. Refunding a $20 order is cheaper than fighting it; a $900 order with strong evidence may be worth contesting.

When a fraud dispute arrives, check whether it qualifies for CE3.0 by looking for two earlier undisputed orders on the same card that share data with the disputed one:.

Recent findings suggest that if you get two matches, pass them to your PSP's CE3.0 evidence fields. On Stripe that's evidence.enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3; other PSPs have their own equivalents. Your adapter handles the mapping. If not, fall back to standard evidence: the IP, receipt, usage logs, renewal reminders and terms acceptance you've been logging all along.

Always submit before the deadline your PSP returns with the dispute. A late response is an automatic loss.

In a recent development, the code above covers the basics. A production system also needs evidence templates per reason code, network deadlines per card brand, retries, and win-rate tracking. That maintenance multiplies with every PSP you add.

According to recent reports, PSP-native tools only see that PSP's data, so they miss the usage logs, renewal reminders and support threads in your own app. A dedicated platform connects to your PSPs and lets you send that data in.

Here's what the buy path looks like with the Chargeflow API. Chargeflow ingests disputes from connected PSPs (Stripe, PayPal, Adyen, Checkout.com, Braintree and 20+ others), fires a dispute.created webhook, and you enrich the dispute with the evidence you logged:.

Chargeflow then builds the response and submits it to the PSP before the deadline. Pre-dispute alerts work the same way: Chargeflow can refund flagged transactions for you, or send alerts.created and alerts.transaction.linked webhooks so your code concerns the refund and reports the result to POST /alerts/{id}/outcome.

Using Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor to build this? Chargeflow publishes its whole developer documentation as one machine-readable file, docs.chargeflow.io/llms-full.txt. Point your assistant at it and it can write the webhook handler and field mapping against the real API, not a guess.

Then your merchants get the disputes, and you need to give them a dispute product without building a dispute team. Chargeflow Connect is built for this. It exposes the same prevention, alerts and recovery engine to your platform in a few delivery models:.

EaaS is the most developer-friendly entry point. You POST /public/2025-04-01/evidence with a merchant account_id and a dispute, get back an in_progress record, and receive an evidence.ready webhook with the PDF link, typically in about 30 seconds. Store the evidence id, not the URL, because the download link expires after 7 days. You can run it on auto-pilot (Chargeflow generates and submits) or co-pilot (your merchant approves first).

In a recent development, don't wait for a customer to dispute a charge to find out your evidence pipeline is broken. Most PSPs give you test cards that create disputes on demand.

One more check before launch: confirm your webhook endpoints verify signatures and return 200 fast. PSPs and Chargeflow retry deliveries that fail, and a slow handler can process the same dispute twice.

Sources indicate that if you only do one thing this week, start logging IP address and device ID on every order. Everything else builds on that data.

True fraud is when a criminal uses a stolen card. Friendly fraud is when the real cardholder makes a purchase, then disputes it. Prevention differs: true fraud is stopped at checkout with risk checks and 3DS, while friendly fraud is won with evidence after the fact.

Recent findings suggest that mostly, yes. Both describe a real cardholder disputing a legitimate charge. "Chargeback fraud" usually implies the customer did it on purpose, while friendly fraud also covers honest mistakes, like a forgotten subscription or a family member's purchase. Visa calls it first-party misuse, and Mastercard calls it first-party fraud.

Recent findings suggest that check the reason code first. For "unauthorized" fraud claims, submit Visa CE3.0 or Mastercard First-Party Trust evidence if the customer qualifies. For "not received" or "canceled" claims, submit delivery proof, usage logs and your cancellation records. For low-value orders, accepting the dispute or refunding on an alert is often cheaper than fighting it.

Industry observers note that partly. 3DS generally shifts liability for fraud disputes to the issuer, so "I didn't authorize this" claims on authenticated payments rarely cost you. It doesn't help with "item not received" or "I canceled" disputes, which need delivery proof and cancellation records.

It has been revealed that no. CE3.0 needs two undisputed purchases on the same card made 120 to 365 days earlier, so it only protects returning customers. For first-time buyers, rely on 3DS and standard evidence.

It has been revealed that yes. Mastercard's First-Party Trust program covers reason code 4837 disputes. It needs one device, one delivery and one extra identity data point, and Mastercard checks them against the cardholder's past purchases. The same evidence table you build for Visa feeds both.

It depends on the stage. At checkout, your PSP's 3D Secure and rules engine. After payment, post-purchase screening such as Chargeflow Prevent holds risky orders before they ship. Before a chargeback, Verifi Order Insight and Ethoca Consumer Clarity show cardholders the order details, while Verifi and Ethoca alerts (offered by many PSPs and by Chargeflow Alerts) and RDR let you refund early. After a chargeback, Visa CE3.0, Mastercard First-Party Trust and dispute automation tools submit the evidence. For developers, the Chargeflow API covers the alert and dispute stages across PSPs, and Chargeflow Connect does the same for platforms.

It has been revealed that the product carousel looks finished. The image fills the card, the price sits under the product name, and the arrow on the right takes you to the next item. The demo goes smoothly.

Then you put the mouse down. You press Tab, and focus skips the arrows entirely. If you rely on a keyboard, the first product is the only one you can reach.

That’s a front-end bug hiding in plain sight. It’s also a good illustration of where AI fits into front-end development. A prompt can describe what a component should look like and what should happen on click. The implementation still has to account for how people reach that control, activate it, and understand what changed.

Imagine asking an AI coding assistant for this:.

According to recent reports, build a React product carousel with previous and next arrows. Show one product at a time and wrap around at the ends.

Here’s an illustrative excerpt from the sort of implementation that can satisfy a quick mouse-driven demo:.

Industry observers note that with some CSS, this can look exactly like the arrow in the design. The click handler advances the slide. A screenshot shows the right layout.

But a plain div sits outside the normal Tab sequence and has no native button semantics or keyboard activation. Adding tabIndex={0} would make it reachable while leaving Enter and Space behavior to be implemented separately. The browser already provides those behaviors through a native button.

Sources indicate that the real omission was in the requirement. “Show arrows” described the visual design. “Let someone reach and operate both controls with a keyboard” describes behavior you can test.

Here’s a small version of the same carousel. The product data is fixed for the example, and the slides change only when the user requests it.

The buttons have visible labels and work with both Enter and Space. When a slide changes, focus stays on the button you pressed, so you can press it again to keep browsing. The status message gives assistive technology a way to announce the upcoming product and its position. Only the current product link is rendered, so Tab never lands on a link from a hidden slide.

It has been revealed that those are deliberate interaction choices. W3C’s carousel pattern provides guidance on using native buttons, keeping focus on the slide controls after activation, and handling automatic rotation when a design requires it. W3C Carousel Pattern.

I’d revise the original prompt like this:.

Build a manual React product carousel. Use native Previous and Next buttons. Both must work with Tab, Enter, and Space. Keep focus on the activated button after a slide change. Announce the newly introduced product name and position through a status message. Keep only the current product link in the Tab sequence. Show what happens when the user advances past the last product.

The extra detail also gives you a review initiative. For this carousel, I’d use four checks:.

AI can help draft automated tests for the active link and wraparound behavior. I’d still run the keyboard and screen reader checks on the integrated page. A global stylesheet can erase a visible focus outline. A surrounding component can introduce an extra tab stop. The experience depends on the page the customer actually uses.

A checkout form can look complete with sample data and lose the customer’s entries when a request fails. A responsive header can match the design at two widths and overlap when a translated label is longer. A component can render correctly in isolation and shift the page when a slow image loads.

According to recent reports, each example gives AI a concrete job. Ask it to preserve form values after a failed request, check the header with longer labels, or reserve space for the image. Then reproduce the condition yourself. Knowing which conditions matter is part of knowing the front end.

Sources indicate that the next time AI gives you a carousel that looks ready, start the review with your hands off the mouse. Tab to Next, press Space twice, and see where focus lands. That short test gives you evidence about how the component works for someone who relies on a keyboard.

How to Reduce Hallucinations in LLMs

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • Ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

Ask one of the newest language models whether a backpack comes in green, and it'll usually admit it doesn't know. Ask it how to return that backpack, and it may send the customer to a returns page, an account screen, and a return label that the store has never had. That's still a hallucination: an answer that sounds right, comes with total confidence, and isn't true.

Whatever you're building, the fix is the same: stop trusting the model with the parts it can get wrong, and check its work before anyone sees it.

In this tutorial we'll build a small support bot for a made-up outdoor gear store, three times over. The first version is the prompt plenty of bots start with. Then we'll apply five fixes, run six tricky customer emails through every version, and finish with a bot where the model can't slip a made-up price, date, or product past the code.

An LLM hallucination is output that's fluent and confident but not backed by the facts: a product that doesn't exist, a policy nobody wrote, a date that's a week out, or a citation to a paper that was never published. The word covers two different failures:.

Each one needs a different fix, so it helps to keep them apart.

A language model writes by predicting likely text, one token at a time. It has no separate store of facts it checks against, and nothing in that process indicates "stop, you don't know this". Training adds to the problem. OpenAI's research on why language models hallucinate points out that when models are graded only on how many answers they get right, a guess scores better than "I don't know", so they learn to guess.

A few things make it worse in your app:.

In a recent development, newer models are much better at the first one. They'll often say they don't know a price rather than invent one. But they still fill gaps with what's typical, and what's typical isn't always what's true for your business. You can't train that out of a model you call through an API. What you can change is what you ask it to do, what you give it, and what you check.

A made-up answer costs more than one bad reply. Some of the costs are already on the record:.

In a support inbox, the cost is quieter but adds up: a refund you didn't owe, or a customer who goes looking for a live chat button that isn't there and doesn't come back.

Northwind Outdoor sells four things: two packs, a rain cover, and a tent. It has two orders on file and three short policies. Here's all of it:.

Six emails come in, and each one is there to trip the bot in a different way:.

According to recent reports, the traps: the 40L pack doesn't come in green, but the 28L does. The 40L is water-resistant, not waterproof. There's no 60L. Whether the return is allowed depends on a membership, a sale price, and a count of days since delivery. The tracking details are in one order record. And the store has no price match policy at all.

Make a folder, add "type": "module" to its package.json, and install the Anthropic SDK and Zod:.

Every version calls the model through one small helper:.

Industry observers note that we're using Claude Opus 5.5 at low effort. These are short, simple replies, so the model doesn't need to think for long. Swap in any model you like, because none of the fixes depend on it.

In a recent development, opus 5.5 didn't invent a single price, colour, or delivery date across the six emails. Every reply stated it couldn't see the store's details. That's real progress compared with older models, but look at what it said instead. Here's the reply to the email about a pack the store doesn't sell:.

It treats the Ridgeline 60L as real and offers to help pick a fit. The other replies made up the store around the customer:.

Northwind has none of those. None of it is a wild guess: it's what a typical online store has. That's exactly why it's dangerous. A customer who goes looking for the live chat or the newsletter discount won't find it, and the bot never answered the question anyway.

The model can't know Northwind's prices, so give them to it. This is the idea behind retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): find the records that matter and put them in the prompt. Our store is small enough to send all of it.

Two things changed. The store data goes in the system prompt, wrapped in tags so the model can tell data from instructions. And the prompt tells it to answer only from that data. Here's the green pack email again:.

Recent findings suggest that right on all three counts, and it even pointed to the pack that does come in green. The return, which needs four facts from two places, came back right as well:.

According to recent reports, delivered October 6, a Trail Club member, so 60 days, so December 5. Bought on sale, so store credit for what was paid, not the list price. Version 2 got all six emails right.

The last line of that prompt matters as much as the data: "If the answer isn't in the data, say you don't know and that a team member will reply by email." Without it, a model that can't find the answer has to choose between letting the customer down and guessing, and training has taught it to guess. With it, "I don't know" is a right answer, not a failure.

The price match email is the test, since the store data indicates nothing about price matching:.

It said it didn't know, passed the question to a person, and answered the parts it could from the data.

If version 2 got everything right, why build a version 3? Because "right on this run" isn't the same as "right every time":.

The next three fixes take the facts and the rules away from the model completely.

According to recent reports, version 3 splits the work into three steps. First, the model reads the email, but instead of writing a reply, it fills in a form. Every field is a choice from a list, a yes or no, or text copied from the email:.

Recent findings suggest that zod describes the form, and z.toJSONSchema() turns it into a JSON schema for the API's structured outputs. The API holds the model to that schema, so product can only be one of our four product IDs, not_sold, or none. There's no way for it to answer ridgeline-60. Zod then checks the answer again, so the rest of the code gets a typed object. SitePoint's guide to LLM structured output with JSON Schema goes deeper on this pattern.

Here's what it read from the 60L email:.

The model is still reading natural language, which it's very good at. It just isn't trusted to know what the store sells anymore.

A form also makes the model's mistakes easy to see. The first time I ran this, the form had no asks_something_else field, and the model filed the price match email under product. The reply didn't make anything up, but the email never reached a person. In version 2, a mistake like that would be hidden inside a paragraph. Here it was one wrong value in a JSON object, and the fix was one more field.

It has been revealed that if all you need from this step is decisions like these, a model built for typed answers can do it faster and for less. Our typed AI pipeline tutorial builds the same kind of email sorter with Jev and Clairic.

Second step: plain code takes the form, looks up the product and the order, applies the rules, and does the maths. What comes out is a list of facts in plain sentences:.

For the return email, that gives:.

Recent findings suggest that every number in there was worked out by code that does the same thing every time, and that you can unit test. The 34 days, the December 5 deadline, and the $151.20 in store credit come out the same on every run, whatever the model does.

Sources indicate that the last rule in decide() matters most. If an email asks something the rules don't cover, the facts say so and the email goes to a person. Code decides when to say "I don't know", not the model.

Third step: the model writes the reply from the facts and nothing else. Writing is the one job here it does better than code.

Even with the right facts, a model writing a reply can still add something: a helpful "ships in 1–2 business days", or a price it remembers from somewhere. So the last step checks the reply. Anything that looks like a number, an order number, or a product name has to appear in the email or the facts:.

It's simple on purpose. It doesn't understand the reply. It just refuses to let through a value that came from nowhere, and that covers the hallucinations that cost money: prices, dates, quantities, and products. Nothing in the reply can talk it out of a result.

The writer runs the check on every draft:.

Industry observers note that if a draft fails, the model gets one retry and is told exactly which values weren't in the facts. If the retry fails too, the customer gets the facts as a plain list. That's less charming, but it's true.

Recent findings suggest that A check like this will raise false alarms, and that's fine. On my first run, it read a line about the tent's 2.1 kg weight as a product called "Weighs 2" and sent the draft back for a retry. The weight was right, and it was the only thing flagged. A false alarm costs a few seconds. A missed one costs a customer. I tightened the patterns (the version above has the fix), but I'd still rather it flag too much than too little.

In a recent development, it's the same thing that separates the better agentic AI coding tools from autocomplete: they run the tests and read the errors instead of trusting their first draft. Model output isn't finished until something other than the model has checked it.

This script sends each email through all three versions, saves every reply, and runs the check from Fix 5 over all of them. Versions 1 and 2 are checked against everything the store knows:.

The check caught one thing in version 1: the "1–2 business days" it made up for processing an order. It missed the "up to 24 hours" for tracking in the same reply, but only because $24 is the rain cover's price, so 24 counted as a known number. And it couldn't catch the invented returns page or live chat at all, because they aren't numbers. That's why the check is the last fix, not the only one.

Reading all 18 replies, here's how each version did:.

Recent findings suggest that version 3 was less helpful than version 2 in one place. It couldn't give the rain cover's price, because decide() only adds facts about the product the email names. Version 2 had the whole store to look at. In version 3, the fix is a rule you write once: when a product has an add-on, include the add-on's facts too.

Here's version 3's reply to the price match email:.

In a recent development, no model is free of hallucinations, so you can't stop one from ever making something up. What you can do is build so a made-up detail can't reach a customer: let code own the facts, and check the model's output against them before it's used. Where it matters, send anything your rules don't cover to a person.

Industry observers note that it cuts them a lot, because the model no longer has to guess facts it was never given. In our test, putting the store's data in the prompt took the bot from no useful answers to six right ones. It doesn't stop the model misreading what it retrieved, mixing up two records, or filling a gap the retrieved text leaves. Pair it with a way out and a check on the output.

Not really. Temperature controls how random the wording is. A low temperature makes the model give the same answer more often, including the same wrong answer.

Collect inputs that have tripped your app (or are likely to), write down the right answer for each, and run every version of your prompt or pipeline over the same set. Automated checks like the one in this tutorial catch made-up values. Read the replies yourself for the rest, because the made-up returns page above would pass any number check.

Hallucinations come from asking a model to do jobs it isn't built for: knowing facts it was never given, and running small programs in its head. The five fixes take those jobs away:.

According to recent reports, the model still does what it's best at: reading messy text and writing a friendly reply. It just isn't trusted with the facts anymore. From here, try a seventh email that asks two things at once, add the add-on rule to decide(), or extend the check to catch colours and sizes as well as numbers.

According to recent reports, LLMs have become essential tools for building software. But for Apple developers, integrating them remains unnecessarily painful.

Developers building AI-powered apps typically take a hybrid approach, adopting some combination of:.

In a recent development, each comes with different APIs, different requirements, different integration patterns. It's a lot, and it adds up quickly. When I interviewed developers about building AI-powered apps, friction with model integration came up immediately. One developer put it bluntly:.

I thought I'd swiftly use the demo for a test and maybe a quick and dirty build but instead wasted so much time. Drove me nuts.

The cost to experiment is high, which discourages developers from discovering that local, open-source models might actually work great for their use case.

Today we're announcing AnyLanguageModel, a Swift package that provides a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework with support for multiple model providers. Our goal is to reduce the friction of working with LLMs on Apple platforms and make it easier to adopt open-source models that run locally.

The core idea is simple: Swap your import statement, keep the same API.

Here's what that looks like in practice. Start with Apple's built-in model:.

Now try an open-source model running locally via MLX:.

AnyLanguageModel supports a range of providers:.

Recent findings suggest that the focus is on local models that you can download from the Hugging Face Hub. Cloud providers are included to lower the barrier to getting started and to provide a migration path. Make it work, then make it right.

When designing AnyLanguageModel, we faced a choice: create a fresh abstraction that tries to capture everything, or build on an existing API. We chose the latter, using Apple's Foundation Models framework as the template.

Recent findings suggest that this might seem counterintuitive. Why tie ourselves to Apple's choices? A few reasons:.

Foundation Models is genuinely well-designed. It leverages Swift features like macros for an ergonomic developer experience, and its abstractions around sessions, tools, and generation map well to how LLMs actually work.

Sources indicate that it's intentionally limited. Foundation Models represents something like a lowest common denominator for language model capabilities. Rather than seeing this as a weakness, we treat it as a stable foundation (hyuk hyuk). Every Swift developer targeting Apple platforms will encounter this API, so building on it directly means less conceptual overhead.

It keeps us grounded. Each additional layer of abstraction takes you further from the problem you're actually solving. Abstractions are powerful, but stack too many and they become a problem in themselves.

The result is that switching between providers requires minimal code changes, and the core abstractions remain clean and predictable.

Industry observers note that one challenge with multi-backend libraries is dependency bloat. If you only want to run MLX models, you shouldn't have to pull in llama.cpp and all its dependencies.

AnyLanguageModel uses Swift 6.1 package traits to solve this. You opt in to only the backends you need:.

Available traits include CoreML, MLX, and Llama (for llama.cpp / llama.swift). By default, no heavy dependencies are included. You get the base API plus cloud providers, which only require standard URLSession networking.

For Xcode projects (which don't yet support trait declarations directly), you can create a small internal Swift package that depends on AnyLanguageModel with the traits you need, then add that package as a local dependency. The README has detailed instructions.

In a recent development, vision-language models are incredibly capable and widely used. They can describe images, extract text from screenshots, analyze charts, and answer questions about visual content. Unfortunately, Apple's Foundation Models framework doesn't currently support sending images with prompts.

Building on an existing API means accepting its constraints. Apple will likely add image support in a future release (iOS 27, perhaps?), but vision-language models are too useful to wait for. So we've extended beyond what Foundation Models offers today.

Here's an example sending an image to Claude:.

It has been revealed that we're taking a calculated risk here; we might design something that conflicts with Apple's eventual implementation. But that's what deprecation warnings are for. Sometimes you have to write the API for the framework that doesn't exist yet.

To see AnyLanguageModel in action, check out chat-ui-swift, a SwiftUI chat application that demonstrates the library's capabilities.

It has been revealed that it's meant as a starting point: Fork it, extend it, swap in different models. See how the pieces fit together and adapt it to your needs.

According to recent reports, anyLanguageModel is presently pre-1.0. The core API is stable, but we're actively working on bringing the full feature set of Foundation Models to all adapters, namely:.

This library is the first step toward something larger. A unified inference API provides the scaffolding needed to build seamless agentic workflows on Apple platforms — applications where models can use tools, access system resources, and accomplish complex tasks. More on that soon. 🤫.

We'd love your help making this better:.

We're excited to see what you build 🦾.

  • Recent findings suggest that this guide explains how text-to-image generators turn words into pixels, why they fail in predictable ways, and how to write prompts that work with the model instead of against it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

According to recent reports, type “a lighthouse on a cliff at dusk, oil painting, warm light” into a text box, wait ten seconds, and a picture that never existed appears. It feels like magic, but it is a well-understood pipeline of language models, neural networks and a great deal of math. Knowing how that pipeline works makes you a better prompter, helps you diagnose bad results, and makes it easier to choose the right tool for a job.

Recent findings suggest that this guide explains how text-to-image generators turn words into pixels, why they fail in predictable ways, and how to write prompts that work with the model instead of against it. It then compares five tools that consistently produce good results, starting with Pollo AI, and finishes with a practical workflow, a troubleshooting table and an FAQ. Aims, credits and model versions change often, so confirm current details on each vendor’s site before you commit to a subscription.

Sources indicate that early image generators were mostly GANs, or generative adversarial networks. A GAN pits two networks against each other: a generator that produces images and a discriminator that tries to spot fakes. GANs could produce sharp faces and textures, but they were hard to train, often collapsed into repeating the same few outputs, and were poor at following free-form text.

A second line of research used autoregressive models, which generate an image piece by piece the way a language model generates words. These handled text prompts better but were slow at high resolution.

It has been revealed that the shift came with diffusion models. Researchers showed that a network trained to reverse a gradual noising process could generate images with excellent quality and diversity, and that it was far more stable to train than a GAN. Combine that with text conditioning and a compressed image representation, and you get the systems behind most of today’s tools. Newer models increasingly swap the traditional convolutional network for transformers, but the core idea of iterative denoising is still the foundation.

In a recent development, under the hood, mainstream generators combine three ideas: a way to understand text, a way to represent images compactly, and a way to generate them gradually. The sections below follow a prompt from keystroke to finished picture.

Neural networks cannot read words, so your prompt is first split into tokens, small chunks of text such as whole words or word fragments. A text encoder then converts those tokens into an embedding, a grid of numbers that captures meaning and context. Many systems use encoders trained jointly on images and their captions, so that the text “a red bicycle” and pictures of red bicycles end up close together in the same mathematical space. Some newer systems add a large language model to understand longer, more detailed instructions.

This is why wording matters. The encoder only sees what you wrote, and it has a limited capacity. A short, specific prompt produces a clear signal. A long, rambling one dilutes each instruction.

Sources indicate that instead of drawing on a blank canvas, the model begins with random static. The pattern of that static is controlled by a seed number. The same prompt with a different seed gives a different image, because it starts from different noise. If a tool lets you fix the seed, you can make results repeatable and change just one variable at a time.

During training, engineers take millions of real images and add noise to them in small steps until only static remains. The network is then trained to predict the noise that was added at each step, which teaches it to reverse the process. At generation time, the model applies that skill to pure noise, removing a little at each step. Because it has learned what real images look like, the “noise” it removes gradually reveals something that looks plausible.

Your text embedding is fed into the network through a mechanism called cross-attention. At each step, parts of the evolving image can “look at” relevant parts of the prompt and adjust accordingly. A region that will become a lighthouse attends to the word “lighthouse”. A region that will become the sky attends to “dusk”.

A setting called classifier-free guidance, often shown as guidance scale or prompt strength, controls how strongly each step is pulled toward the prompt. The model computes one prediction with the prompt and one without it, then exaggerates the difference. A low value gives the model freedom and often more natural, varied results. A high value follows the words more literally but can produce oversaturated, over-sharpened or distorted images.

Running diffusion directly on full-resolution pixels would be very expensive. The idea behind Stable Diffusion, known as latent diffusion, is to compress images into a much smaller latent representation using an autoencoder. Denoising happens in that compact space, and a decoder turns the final latent back into a full image. This is a major reason high-quality generation now runs in seconds on a cloud GPU instead of minutes.

Industry observers note that the number of denoising steps and the scheduler, which decides how much noise to remove at each step, shape the speed and look of the result. More steps usually add detail up to a point, then give diminishing returns. Many tools hide these settings, but the trade-off is always the same: fewer steps are faster and cheaper, more steps can look more refined.

Most pipelines finish with an upscaler or refinement pass that sharpens detail and fixes small artifacts. Many tools also offer inpainting, which regenerates only a selected region, outpainting, which extends the canvas, and variations, which restart from a related image.

According to recent reports, A generator can only produce what it has learned to represent. Models are trained on very large collections of images paired with captions, and the quality, diversity and licensing of that data affect both the output and the legal picture. Models trained on more photographs tend to produce convincing photorealism. Models tuned on illustration and concept art lean toward painterly looks.

Recent findings suggest that this also explains a few behaviors. Common subjects look great because the model has seen thousands of examples. Rare or very specific subjects, such as an unusual machine part or a niche cultural item, often look generic or wrong. Biases in the data can show up as stereotypes, for example in how “a doctor” or “a CEO” is depicted, so it helps to describe the people and setting you actually want.

Understanding the process explains the familiar failures:.

Pollo AI’s text to image AI is a browser-based generator built around a simple loop: write a prompt, pick a style, generate, and download. Its page highlights HD output and a wide range of looks, from photorealistic scenes to cute cartoons, anime, pencil sketches, isometric art, abstract compositions and surreal visuals. Files can be downloaded as WebP, PNG or JPEG, a practical spread for web work: WebP keeps pages light, PNG preserves clean edges and transparency-friendly graphics, and JPEG works almost everywhere.

Pollo is also part of a wider platform that covers AI video, so a still image you like can become the starting point for motion without switching ecosystems. That matters for teams producing social content, because one workflow can cover both the image and the short clip built from it.

Things to check: the page does not list specific model names or credit amounts, so review the current strategy details before relying on it for high-volume work. Commercial use requires a paid plan.

Best for: quick, versatile image generation across many styles, especially if you also plan to make video.

Midjourney has built its reputation on strong aesthetics. Images tend to arrive with polished composition, dramatic lighting and a distinctive painterly feel, which is why it is popular for concept art, mood boards, album-style visuals and editorial illustration. It offers style references and personalization, so you can steer results toward a consistent look across a project. It also supports editing and variation tools for refining a chosen image.

In a recent development, the trade-offs are practical. It is a paid service, and its prompts reward experimentation over literal instruction following, so you sometimes get something beautiful that is not exactly what you described.

Best for: artistic, high-impact visuals where mood matters more than exact specification.

Adobe Firefly focuses on professional workflows and commercial confidence. Adobe describes Firefly’s own models as trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public-domain material, and it attaches Content Credentials metadata that records AI involvement. It connects with tools many teams already use, including Photoshop features like generative fill and generative expand, which suits designers who edit as much as they generate.

Recent findings suggest that firefly also provides controls such as style and composition references. Its results can feel cleaner and more commercial than Midjourney’s, which is an advantage for marketing assets and a limitation if you want a wild artistic look.

Best for: marketing and design teams that need editing tools and clearer licensing.

Ideogram is known for rendering legible text inside images, a task where many generators struggle. That makes it a strong choice for posters, social graphics, logo concepts, packaging mockups and product visuals that need a headline or short phrase to read correctly. It also offers style controls and a community gallery that doubles as a prompt library.

Even so, long paragraphs of on-image text can still go wrong. Keep the copy to a few words, put it in quotation marks in the prompt, and describe the lettering style.

Best for: graphics that combine imagery with short, readable text.

In a recent development, leonardo AI is built for creators who want more control. It offers multiple models, fine-tuning options, image-to-image guidance and a canvas for editing, with a particular following among game artists and designers who need consistent characters and assets. Features such as reference-based generation help keep a character recognizable across many scenes.

The wide set of options is powerful but means a steeper learning curve than a one-box generator, and credit systems can take time to understand.

Best for: consistent characters, game and concept assets, and consumers who like tuning settings.

According to recent reports, A reliable prompt has five parts. Put the most crucial part first, because it often carries the most weight.

Compare weak prompts with stronger ones:.

How do text-to-image generators work? They convert your prompt into a numerical representation, then use a diffusion model to remove noise from a random starting image step by step, guided by that representation, until a matching picture appears.

Which text-to-image tool is best? It depends on the job. Pollo AI suits fast, varied generation, Midjourney suits artistic work, Adobe Firefly suits commercial design, Ideogram suits images with text and Leonardo AI suits tuned, consistent assets.

Why does the same prompt give different results? Each run starts from a different random seed. Fixing the seed, where a tool allows it, makes results more repeatable.

In a recent development, can I use AI-generated images commercially? Often yes, but the rules differ by tool and blueprint. Pollo, for example, notes that commercial use requires a paid plan. Always check the current terms.

It has been revealed that how do I get readable text in an AI image? Use a tool strong at text, keep the wording to a few words, and add the text in a design editor if accuracy is critical.

In a recent development, what file format should I download? WebP for lightweight web pages, PNG for graphics and sharp edges, JPEG for broad compatibility.

Can I turn a generated image into a video? Many platforms support it. Pollo AI, for example, also covers AI video, so you can move from a still to motion in one place.

Recent findings suggest that text-to-image generators work by turning language into numbers and using those numbers to guide a model that denoises random static into a picture. Once you understand that, prompts stop being guesswork: you give the model a clear subject, style and lighting, you iterate one change at a time, and you fix small flaws locally. Start with a versatile option such as Pollo AI, then add Midjourney, Firefly, Ideogram or Leonardo when a project needs their particular strengths.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, while everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up upcoming ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show.
  • Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other key tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.
  • It has been revealed that over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, while everyone (and their grandma 👵) is spinning up upcoming ASR models, picking the right one for your use case can feel more overwhelming than choosing your next Netflix show. As of 21 Nov 2025, there are 150 Audio-Text-to-Text and 27K ASR models on the Hub 🤯.

Most benchmarks focus on short-form English transcription (<30s), and overlook other key tasks, such as (1) multilingual performance and (2) model throughput, which can a be deciding factor for long-form audio like meetings and podcasts.

It has been revealed that over the past two years, the Open ASR Leaderboard has become a standard for comparing open and closed-source models on both accuracy and efficiency. Recently, multilingual and long-form transcription tracks have been added to the leaderboard 🎉.

As of 21 Nov 2025, the Open ASR Leaderboard compares 60+ open and closed-source models from 18 organizations, across 11 datasets.

In a recent preprint, we dive into the technical setup and highlight some key trends in modern ASR. Here are the big takeaways 👇.

Models combining Conformer encoders with large language model (LLM) decoders right now lead in English transcription accuracy. For example, NVIDIA’s Canary-Qwen-2.5B, IBM’s Granite-Speech-3.3-8B, and Microsoft’s Phi-4-Multimodal-Instruct achieve the lowest word error rates (WER), showing that integrating LLM reasoning can significantly boost ASR accuracy.

💡 Pro-tip: NVIDIA introduced Fast Conformer, a 2x faster variant of the Conformer, that is used in their Canary and Parakeet suite of models.

Recent findings suggest that while highly accurate, these LLM decoders tend to be slower than simpler approaches. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, efficiency is measured using inverse real-time factor (RTFx), where higher is better.

For even faster inference, CTC and TDT decoders deliver 10–100× faster throughput, albeit with slightly higher error rates. This makes them ideal for real-time, offline, or batch transcription tasks (such as meetings, lectures, or podcasts).

It has been revealed that openAI’s Whisper Large v3 remains a strong multilingual baseline, supporting 99 languages. However, fine-tuned or distilled variants like Distil-Whisper and CrisperWhisper often outperform the original on English-only tasks, showing how targeted fine-tuning can improve specialization (how to fine-tune? Check out guides for Whisper, Parakeet, and Voxtral).

That said, focusing on English tends to reduce multilingual coverage 👉 a classic case of the tradeoff between specialization and generalization. Similarly, while self-supervised systems like Meta’s Massively Multilingual Speech (MMS) and Omnilingual ASR can support 1K+ languages, they trail behind language-specific encoders in accuracy.

⭐ While just five languages are at the moment benchmarked, we’re planning to expand to more languages and are excited for newly introduced dataset and models contributions to multilingual ASR through GitHub pull requests.

According to recent reports, 🎯 Alongside multilingual benchmarks, several community-driven leaderboards focus on individual languages. For example, the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard compares models across Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, highlighting how speech variation and diglossia challenge current systems. Similarly. the Russian ASR Leaderboard provides a growing hub for evaluating encoder-decoder and CTC models on Russian-specific phonology and morphology. These localized efforts mirror the broader multilingual leaderboard’s mission to encourage dataset sharing, fine-tuned checkpoints, and transparent model comparisons, especially in languages with fewer established ASR resources.

Recent findings suggest that for long-form audio (e.g., podcasts, lectures, meetings), closed-source systems still edge out open ones. It could be due to domain tuning, custom chunking, or production-grade optimization.

Among open models, OpenAI’s Whisper Large v3 performs the best. But for throughput, CTC-based Conformers shine 👉 for example, NVIDIA’s Parakeet CTC 1.1B achieves an RTFx of 2793.75, compared to 68.56 for Whisper Large v3, with only a moderate WER degradation (6.68 and 6.43 respectively).

The tradeoff? Parakeet is English-only, again reminding us of that multilingual and specialization tradeoff 🫠.

⭐ While closed systems still lead, there’s huge potential for open-source innovation here. Long-form ASR remains one of the most exciting frontiers for the community to tackle next!

Given how fast ASR is evolving, we’re excited to see what newly introduced architectures push performance and efficiency, and how the Open ASR Leaderboard continues to serve as a transparent, community-driven benchmark for the field, and as a reference for other leaderboards (Russian, Arabic, and Speech DeepFake Detection).

We’ll keep expanding the Open ASR LeaderBoard with more models, more languages, and more datasets so stay tuned 👀.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments.
  • Industry observers note that when fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics.
  • RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that hugging Face TRL now officially integrates with RapidFire AI to accelerate your fine-tuning and post-training experiments. TRL users can now discover, install, and run RapidFire AI as the fastest way to compare multiple fine-tuning/post-training configurations to customize LLMs without major code changes and without bloating GPU requirements.

Industry observers note that when fine-tuning or post-training LLMs, teams often do not have the time and/or budget to compare multiple configs even though that can significantly boost eval metrics. RapidFire AI lets you launch multiple TRL configs concurrently--even on a single GPU--and compare them in near real time via a new adaptive, chunk-based scheduling and execution scheme. In internal benchmarks referenced in the TRL page, this delivers ~16–24× higher experimentation throughput than sequentially comparing configs one after another, enabling you to reach much better metrics much faster.

RapidFire AI establishes live three-way communication between your IDE, a metrics dashboard, and a multi-GPU execution backend.

Drop-in TRL wrappers — Use RFSFTConfig, RFDPOConfig, and RFGRPOConfig as near-zero-code replacements for TRL's SFT/DPO/GRPO configs.

Adaptive chunk-based concurrent training — RapidFire AI shards the dataset into a given number of chunks and cycles configs at chunk boundaries to enable earlier apples-to-apples comparisons and also maximize GPU utilization.

Interactive Control Ops (IC Ops) — From the dashboard itself, you can Stop, Resume, Delete, and Clone-Modify, possibly with Warm-Start, any runs in flight to avoid wasting resources on underperforming configs and double-down on better performing configs--no job restarts, no juggling separate GPUs or clusters, no resource bloat.

Clone promising configurations with modified hyperparameters, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights, all from the live dashboard.

Multi-GPU orchestration — The RapidFire AI scheduler automatically places and orchestrates configs across available GPUs on chunks of data via effcient shared-memory mechanisms. You focus on your models and eval metrics, not plumbing.

In a recent development, MLflow-based dashboard — Real-time metrics, logs, and IC Ops in one place as soon as you start your experiment. Support for more dashboards such as Trackio, W&B, and TensorBoard coming soon.

It has been revealed that rapidFire AI splits your dataset randomly into "chunks" and cycles LLM configurations through the GPUs at chunk boundaries. You get incremental signal on eval metrics across all configs much more quickly. The automatic checkpointing via an efficient shared-memory-based adapter/model spilling/loading mechanism keeps training smooth, stable, and consistent. Use IC Ops to adapt mid-flight to stop low-performers earlier and clone promising ones with tweaked config knobs, optionally warm-starting from the parent's weights.

Sequential vs. Task Parallel vs. RapidFire AI: The adaptive scheduler maximizes GPU utilization across multiple configs and GPUs. The bottom row shows IC Ops in action—stopping, cloning, and modifying runs mid-flight.

Building Reliable Product Emails Into Your Application

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • A password reset email is part of your login flow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Sources indicate that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

A password reset email is part of your login flow. An invoice notification is part of your billing experience. Yet development teams often treat these messages as background tasks: render a template, call a sending API, and move on. That approach leaves an vital part of the product experience untested until a user cannot complete the action they started.

Sources indicate that testing the application interface alone leaves a gap. A successful request to an email provider does not establish that the recipient can find the message, understand it, or use its links. Product emails need explicit success criteria, useful diagnostic records, and recovery options when something fails.

It has been revealed that A reliable workflow combines application tests, controlled mailbox checks, and pre-send diagnostics for authentication and inbox placement. A comparison of available tools can help you identify which checks your existing setup covers and where additional testing would be useful. The goal is to investigate specific gaps rather than add another service without a clear purpose.

Start with the action the recipient needs to complete. A weekly activity summary can tolerate a delay that would make a sign-in code useless. An invoice needs accurate amounts and a clear payment destination. A security alert needs enough context for someone to recognize the event without exposing sensitive information.

Recent findings suggest that for each message, document its trigger, expected timing, required data, and expiration behavior. Decide what the application should display if submission fails or the user requests another copy. These decisions give developers and testers concrete acceptance criteria.

For a password reset, test the complete journey: requesting the message, receiving it in a controlled mailbox, following the link, and setting a latest password. Also check what happens when the link expires or has already been used.

Template tests should cover the data your application actually encounters. Try long names, missing optional fields, non-Latin characters, and large order totals. Escape user-provided values appropriately, and make sure conditional sections disappear cleanly when their data is absent.

Sources indicate that inspect both HTML and plain-text versions. Instructions should remain understandable when images are blocked, while descriptive links and readable text should make the next action clear. Check that every URL points to the correct environment, especially when staging and production share template code.

Recent findings suggest that A development sandbox lets you inspect generated messages without contacting customers. Use it to check headers, attachments, and content. Keep a separate rendering check for the email clients your audience uses, because a sandbox preview cannot reproduce every client’s behavior.

Industry observers note that A background queue can prevent a slow sending API from delaying a web request. It also creates another failure boundary: a worker may time out after the provider has accepted the email but before your application records the result.

If the job retries blindly, the recipient may receive two messages. Assign a stable identifier to each logical notification and record the provider’s message identifier when available. Where supported, reuse an idempotency key for retries of the same send operation, following the provider’s documented retention window.

Sources indicate that distinguish retries from intentional resends. A user asking for a newly introduced reset link is a different event from a worker repeating an uncertain request. Define which link remains valid when another is issued, and test that behavior explicitly.

It has been revealed that retries also need limits. Temporary service failures may justify another attempt with backoff. A permanently invalid address needs a correction or suppression workflow, rather than repeated sending.

According to recent reports, provider events describe different stages of the sending process. An acceptance response means the provider accepted the request. A delivery event generally means the receiving mail server accepted the message; it does not prove inbox placement or that a person read it.

Capture the events your provider exposes, including bounces, delays, and complaints. Associate them with the original notification so support staff can investigate a particular report. Confirm each event’s documented meaning instead of treating similar labels across providers as interchangeable.

Webhook handlers should verify incoming requests using the provider’s documented mechanism and tolerate duplicate notifications. Avoid assuming events always arrive in chronological order. Record enough history to explain what happened without allowing a late event to overwrite a more informative state.

According to recent reports, before releasing a significant template or infrastructure change, send controlled messages through the production sending configuration to test accounts at commonly used mailbox providers. Use synthetic data, and check placement, rendering, link behavior, and how long the message takes to arrive.

In a recent development, inspect authentication results in the received headers. Published DNS records are only part of the configuration; the actual message must use the expected signing domain and sending infrastructure. If you change providers or domains, repeat these checks rather than assuming the previous results still apply.

Sources indicate that treat test mailbox results as samples. They can reveal problems, but they cannot guarantee identical placement for every recipient. Mailbox settings, filtering decisions, and recipient history can produce different outcomes.

Provide a resend option with sensible rate limits and explain when users should expect the message. Where appropriate, let signed-in users verify or correct their address. For public account-recovery forms, avoid responses that reveal whether a particular address has an account.

Give support staff a way to distinguish a notification that was never generated from a failed submission or a message accepted by the receiving server. Protect that diagnostic access, limit retention, and avoid logging reset tokens, private message bodies, or unnecessary personal information.

According to recent reports, reliable product email depends on the whole journey, from the triggering event to the recipient’s next action. Testing each stage and making failures observable helps teams resolve problems before owners repeatedly click resend or abandon the task.

Building Deep Research: How we Achieved State of the Art

📅 24 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important applications of AI.
  • The task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling.
  • This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that research agents are rapidly becoming one of the most important applications of AI. Research is a foundational knowledge-work task: collecting, reading, and synthesizing information underpins everything from writing and decision-making to coding itself. Yet human-driven research is constrained by memory, reading speed, and time. AI research agents, by contrast, can process vast amounts of information, synthesize insights instantly, and scale effortlessly. Because of this, research agents are emerging as a top use case for AI today and will soon become a core subcomponent of broader agentic workflows across content generation, coding, sales, and more. In this post, we share the technical and philosophical lessons we’ve learned building a state-of-the-art research agent, and where we believe the field is headed.

The task of building an agent harness is to create a software layer that enhances a model’s runtime execution through context management, tool invocations, loop control, orchestration, and error handling. Building applications on top of rapidly improving models is, however, a modern engineering challenge. How can we design software today that absorbs the performance gains from future model releases?

This requires forecasting how models will evolve, staying optimistic about their progress, limiting assumptions, and avoiding hand-crafted optimizations.

We learned this the hard way seven months ago, when we had to abandon our first attempt at deep research and rebuild the entire system from scratch. The first architecture was complicated and sophisticated (we thought this was a good thing), but its assumptions became bottlenecks when the next generation of models arrived.

It has been revealed that over the last seven months, model capabilities have quietly but meaningfully evolved (especially in their tool-calling abilities). This single optimization focus has pushed us from workflows to agents. We believe future models will be trained to solve the current pain points of agent developers. Every model is ultimately consumed by a harness, so models should evolve in service of that harness. We hope to see models improve in high-recall summarization (for context compression), tool-calling reliability, and concision in writing.

In a recent development, similarly, tools should evolve to support LLMs and widely adopted agent harnesses. The best tools should perform some context engineering on the tool side, abstracted away from the agent. They should return only the most relevant data instead of dumping large volumes of tokens into the context window. As a tool provider, we’ve invested heavily in our advanced search feature, which has context engineering baked in. This in turn lowers hallucinations and latency for the downstream agent processes.

To build agents that improve over time, we followed a few guiding principles:.

According to recent reports, long-horizon research tasks expose a fundamental challenge in current agent design: the task of maintaining a clean, optimized context window over time. If curating context is not a task the engineer pays close attention to, the agent is almost destined for failure. The following outlines our thinking around this concept within the deep research domain.

Using Tavily’s Advanced Search is the natural first step to take in overcoming this challenge, in that it abstracts away the processing of raw web content and returns only the most relevant content chunks from each source. In leveraging this functionality, we let Tavily Search do the heavy lifting and allow Tavily Research to reap the benefit, gathering the most valuable content in a latency-efficient manner.

Ensuring that the agent does not overfit to a single research thread is the next step towards an effective context-gathering pipeline. It is in this regard that global state persistence and source deduplication is paramount, and in our case, it helps threefold:.

Industry observers note that at Tavily, interacting with the web is our bread and butter. Architecting a refined web-retrieval system engineered for deep research was a foundational building block for our deep research agent design as a whole.

Recent findings suggest that humans research in an inherently unstructured, iterative way. We start by defining the task: what we’re trying to accomplish and what information we need. We next gather data from our sources, extracting the key insights and holding them in short-term memory, letting these distilled thoughts guide our subsequent actions.

It has been revealed that this cycle repeats: collect information, distill it, decide what to do next. Only once we’ve gathered enough understanding to produce the final deliverable do we return to the original sources, using them as references to assemble the finished product.

It has been revealed that we believe that deep research agents should be designed in a similar manner, in that tool outputs should be distilled into reflections, and only the set of past reflections should be used as context for your tool caller. Similar to humans, it is only at the point when your agent begins to prepare the final deliverable that you must provide the raw information as context, so as to ensure there is no information loss.

Recent findings suggest that this approach differs from traditional context structuring in a ReAct agent-based architecture. Typically, tool calls and outputs are propagated through the tool calling loop, with previously retrieved/generated tokens being persisted in the context window on each subsequent iteration. This pattern can be seen in LangChain’s Open Deep Research agent implementation, and from a token consumption perspective, it can be modeled by the following quadratic series, where n n n is the amount of tokens the tool calling model is invoked with on each tool calling iteration, and m m m is the number of tool calling iterations.

n+2n+3n+⋯+mn  =  n⋅m(m+1)2n + 2n + 3n + \cdots + mn \;=\; n \cdot \frac{m(m+1)}{2}n+2n+3n+⋯+mn=n⋅2m(m+1)​.

Contrarily, our proposed method of context engineering removes this token propagation (as the knowledge distillations, even when aggregated, are negligible when compared to the quantity of tokens gathered from web) and can be modeled by the following linear series.

n+n+n+⋯+n  =  nmn + n + n + \cdots + n \;=\; nmn+n+n+⋯+n=nm.

When comparing the two approaches, tokens are saved on a per-agent basis by a factor of m+12 \frac{m+1}{2} 2m+1​, and when extrapolating this over a multi-agent system and with consumption at scale, the absolute value of tokens saved becomes even more significant.

Through this methodology, we were able to reduce token consumption by 66% (when compared to Open Deep Research) while achieving SOTA on DeepResearch Bench – the intersection of quality and efficiency in full effect.

Industry observers note that building production-grade agents is a balancing act. We leaned into autonomy to maximize performance and quality, while still meeting strict requirements for latency, cost, and reliability.

According to recent reports, LLMs are inherently non-deterministic, and we found that giving them guard-railed freedom to reason and iterate produces the strongest results. Autonomy, when gone wrong, can cause agent behavior to go off track. Tools can be called incorrectly, LLMs can overfit to a subtopic, and expected reasoning patterns may break. No single safeguard will catch all of these concerns.

In a recent development, A shift in engineering mindset is required: treat failure modes as core design considerations, not afterthoughts. Simple guardrails like tool-call retries or model cascades help, but proactively anticipating anomalies, reinforcing proper patterns in prompting and edge-case testing is what enables production-grade, long-running agents.

Industry observers note that from our experience, it’s better to expose a small, essential toolset to the agent rather than a large, complex one. We were tempted to over-engineer by adding many tools that seemed useful in theory, but in practice this created newly introduced failure modes and made it harder for LLMs to consistently choose the right tool and iterate effectively.

Sources indicate that we used evals to steer our development process but also recognize their shortcomings. LLM-as-a-judge evals are difficult to trust: current models are non‑deterministic, uninterpretable in their reasoning, and can turn into bottlenecks, especially for long‑running agents where a single experiment can take days to complete.

Rather than optimizing for benchmark scores, we optimized for directional feedback. The core question was always: did this change make the agent more reliable and more useful in practice? Evals became a tool for validating that direction, not the optimization target. Intuition and careful agent‑trace monitoring consistently provided higher‑signal feedback than any single eval score. Overall, the best outcome is rarely the highest numerical score. For production systems, improvements like reduced token usage, reliability, lower latency, and fewer failures are more valuable than a one‑point bump on an eval.

It has been revealed that what is r in your solution ? Is it a scratch pad that is updated in the LLM context between each round of research ?

r in the solution is the research insight from previous tool call.

A great insight on getting more by doing less.
