Continuous batching from first principles

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.
  • If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency.
  • Industry observers note that this generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: in this blog post, starting from attention mechanisms and KV caching, we derive continuous batching by optimizing for throughput.

If you've ever used Qwen, Claude, or any other AI chatbot, you've probably noticed something: it takes a while for the first word of the response to appear, and then words appear one-by-one on your screen with (hopefully) a regular and fast-paced frequency. That's because at the heart of it, all LLMs are just fancy next token predictors. An LLM first processes your entire prompt to produce one new token. Then it keeps adding tokens one by one, each time reading everything that came before, until it decides generation is over.

Industry observers note that this generation process is computationally expensive: it requires passing the input through billions of parameters for each token generated. To make these models practical for real-world applications, particularly when serving many customers simultaneously, researchers and engineers have developed a range of efficient inference techniques.One of the most impactful optimizations is continuous batching, which attempts to maximize performance by processing multiple conversations in parallel and swapping them out when they are done.

To understand how continuous batching works and why it's so effective in high-load serving scenarios, we'll build up from the fundamentals of how LLMs process tokens.

The attention mechanism is the central piece of how LLMs work. A language model processes text by breaking it down into pieces that we call tokens. We can conceptually think of "tokens" as "words", but sometimes a word might be composed of several tokens. For each token sequence, the network computes a prediction of what the next token should be.

Many operations in the network are token-wise: each token is processed independently, and the output for a given token depends only on that token's content, not on any other tokens in the sequence. Operations like this include layer normalization or matrix multiplication. However, to create connections between words in a sentence, we need operations where tokens can influence each other.

It has been revealed that this is where attention comes in. Attention layers are the only place where different tokens interact with each other. Understanding how a network connects tokens together means understanding attention.

Let's see how this works in practice, in the case where there is only one input prompt.

It has been revealed that consider the initial prompt I am sure this project, tokenized as 7 tokens: [, I, am, sure, this, pro, ject]. The , or "Beginning of Sequence", is a special token we add at the start of the prompt to tell the language model that a upcoming conversation starts here.

Each token is represented inside the network with a vector of length d (the hidden dimension). Therefore, the seven incoming tokens form a tensor xxx with shape [1,7,d]\left[1, 7, d \right][1,7,d]. 1 is the number of sequences, or batch size, which is just one in our case. 7 is the sequence length, and d is the hidden dimension, or the size of each token representation. Going forward, we'll use nnn instead of 7 as the sequence length.

It has been revealed that input tensor x x x is then projected by three matrices: the query projection Wq W_q Wq​, the key projection Wk W_k Wk​ and the value projection Wv W_v Wv​. This produces three tensors Q Q Q, K K K and V V V, all of shape [1,n,A] \left[1, n , A \right] [1,n,A], where A A A is the dimension of the attention head. We call them the query, key and value states, respectively. This is represented on the left in the figure below.

Next, tensors Q Q Q and K K K are multiplied together to measure similarity between tokens, producing a tensor of shape [1,n,n] \left[ 1, n , n \right] [1,n,n]. This is why we say that attention has quadratic complexity in sequence length. Computing QKT QK^T QKT requires O(n2d) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 d \right) O(n2d) operations, so the cost is a square of n n n the sequence length. It is represented on the right in the figure above.

In a recent development, we then apply a boolean attention mask to QKT QK^T QKT to control which tokens can interact, as represented in the figure below. In this figure, the attention mask is a causal mask, meaning each token only interacts with tokens that came before it. This follows the intuition that a cause must come before its consequence, hence the name causal mask. The attention mask is crucial because it dictates all token interactions in the network. Set all attention mask values to False and no token will ever interact with another in the whole network. We'll examine attention masks more closely in a few paragraphs.

According to recent reports, finally, after applying the attention mask, we take a token-wise softmax (which is the same as saying a row-wise softmax) and multiply the result by the value projection V V V to get the output of one attention head, of shape [1,n,A] \left[ 1, n , A \right] [1,n,A]. We offer a visual summary of the whole process in the following figure.

We are going to use a lot of attention visualization in this post, so to simplify things, we are going to condense the figure above just a bit.

Why this matters: In continuous batching, Q Q Q, K K K, and V V V can have different numbers of tokens because, as we'll see, we'll be processing different stages (prefill and decode) at the same time. To make it more general, let's say Q Q Q has shape [1,nQ,A] \left[1, n_Q , A \right] [1,nQ​,A], K K K has shape [1,nK,A] \left[ 1, n_K , A \right] [1,nK​,A], and V V V has shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A].

The attention scores QKT QK^T QKT then have shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​], and the attention mask has the same shape since it's applied point-wise to the scores.

After applying the attention mask and row-wise softmax, we multiply by V V V. Since we're multiplying a matrix of shape [1,nQ,nK] \left[ 1, n_Q , n_K \right] [1,nQ​,nK​] by one of shape [1,nV,A] \left[ 1, n_V , A \right] [1,nV​,A], the inner dimensions must match: nK=nV n_K = n_V nK​=nV​. This means V V V and K K K always have the same length, so we can simplify our visualizations by only showing K K K.Don't worry if this seems abstract: the figures will make it concrete.

Furthermore, since we know that the attention mask is applied to QKT QK^T QKT, we know they have the same shape. Instead of representing the attention scores, we will represent the attention mask in its place. Finally, since Q Q Q, K K K and V V V are direct projections of x x x, no need to represent x x x. This gives the simplified figure where we only represent Q Q Q, K K K and the attention mask:.

This representation also underlines how we can read an attention mask.

Sources indicate that we read the mask row-by-row, which is the same as reading token-by-token: each row corresponds to one token's attention computation. A green square at position (row i, column j) means True: token j can influence token i. A white square means False: no interaction allowed.

According to recent reports, for example, look at the third row for token "am". The "I" column is green, so "I" influences the computation of "am". The "pro" column is white, so "pro" doesn't influence "am" . This is causal masking at work: future tokens can't affect past ones.

The last layer of the model outputs a token prediction for each input token. In our context, generating the continuation of a single prompt, we only care about the next token prediction from the last token. The last token is "ject" in the figure above, and the associated prediction is "will".

It has been revealed that the process we just described, where we take an entire input sequence, pass it through multiple attention layers and compute a score for the next token, is called prefill. This is because, as we'll see in a moment, much of the computation we performed can be cached and reused – hence, we are prefilling the cache. Thanks to the use of this cache, sequence generation can proceed using much less compute in a phase called decoding. In the decoding phase, generating one latest token will be much faster than the initial full-sequence computation. Let's see why.

To continue generation, we begin a new forward pass, which would naively look like this:.

In a recent development, to compute the attention scores of the newly introduced token, we still need the key and value projections of the previous tokens. So we need to repeat the matrix multiplication of the old tokens (in grey in the figure above) with Wk W_k Wk​ and Wv W_v Wv​ to retrieve a result that was already computed once before. In other terms, we are wasting compute. Let's see how we can avoid that.

Right off the bat, we notice that the last token does not impact the attention calculation of the other tokens:.

This follows the idea of the causal mask: since "will" comes after all previous tokens, it does not change their attention calculation. For text generation, causal attention is by far the most common, so we will focus on that case from now on. Keep in mind that non-causal attention schemes can also be used, especially when dealing with images. Considering we only need the next-token prediction for the "will" token, we can simplify the attention mechanism by only computing the output for this token.

It has been revealed that moreover, we already computed the K K K and V V V states for the tokens "", … , "ject" during the previous forward pass: if they have been stored, we do not need to recompute them again. This is the KV cache: the list of key and value states created during generation. It essentially allows one to reduce the compute cost of generating token n+1 n+1 n+1 from O(n2) \mathcal{O} \left( n^2 \right) O(n2) to O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n) by avoiding recomputation of key and value projections, while paying a memory cost of O(n) \mathcal{O} \left( n \right) O(n).

In a recent development, in the figure above, only the tokens in white are computed: instead of computing the keys and values for 8 tokens, we compute them for 1. You can see that through KV caching, a lot of compute is saved.You can check this post for more visualizations of KV caching, or this one for a practical implementation example.

Recent findings suggest that let's be a bit more specific about the cache size, because it's a good opportunity to examine the shapes present in our model. For a model with L \mathcal L L attention layers and H H H attention heads with head dimension A A A, the total cache size needed to store one token will be 2∗L∗AH 2 *\mathcal L * AH 2∗L∗AH with a factor of 2 2 2 to account for both K K K and V V V.For instance, Llama-2-7B with L=32 \mathcal{L}=32 L=32 layers, H=32 H=32 H=32 heads, and A=128 A=128 A=128 requires 2×32×128=8,192 2 \times 32 \times 128 = 8,192 2×32×128=8,192 values per token per layer. With float16 precision, this takes 2AH×2 2AH \times 2 2AH×2 bytes =16 = 16 =16 KB in memory.

In a recent development, KV caching is useful when we want to generate the next token, which is a stage we call decoding. But it can also be useful in the prefill stage, when we process the initial prompt and have many input tokens. Especially when there are large initial prompts that don't fit in GPU memory all at once.

Up till now, we have looked at an example of prefill where we have n=7 n=7 n=7 tokens, but in practice initial prompts can be much longer. For instance, when using Cursor, you can add your repository to the prompt, where it acts as context: this significantly increases the prompt size. In such cases, the memory needed to store the activations for n n n tokens can be larger than the available memory on the GPU. Thus we cannot perform prefill in a single forward pass: we have to split the prefill in chunks. This is called chunked prefill, and it's going to be one of the components needed to enable efficient inference.

Let's pretend that the available memory is very constrained, and that we can only pass m=4 m=4 m=4 tokens per forward pass. If we have an initial prompt with n=7 n = 7 n=7 tokens, we need to split it in ⌈n/m⌉=2 \lceil n /m \rceil = 2 ⌈n/m⌉=2 chunks (rounding up 7/4 = 1.75 to 2). We illustrate the example below using the same n n n and m m m notations:.

We can do that thanks to the KV cache. We store the KV states during the first prefill split, and during the second prefill split, we prepend the stored KV states to the new KV states. We also adapt the attention mask accordingly. Visually, it looks like we split the non-chunked prefill in the middle.

The key insight: cached KV states let us process the prompt incrementally without losing information.

Although we highlighted here an example where we split the prefill into 2 chunks, chunked prefill can be used to split the prefill in any way we want, adapting flexibly to memory constraints.

We are now finally equipped with all the tools we need to understand Continuous Batching.

In our previous examples we have only considered the case of batch size one, i.e. we only generate tokens for one prompt at a time. In the context of evaluation or model serving, we want to generate tokens for a large number of prompts. To increase the throughput, which is the number of tokens generated per second, the best course of action is to generate tokens in parallel for a batch of several prompts.

To batch prompts together, the naive way is to add an axis to both input tensors: token sequence and attention mask. However, this comes with a constraint on the shape of the inputs: we need all prompts to have the same length, because tensors must be rectangular. To achieve this, we usually add padding on the left so the latest token prediction always comes from the rightmost token. We also modify the attention mask of each prompt accordingly, as shown below:.

Industry observers note that where the padding tokens are coloured in orange. Then we can perform the forward pass as we used to, with the added dimension of the batch size. This is called batched generation: efficient for same-length prompts, but wasteful when lengths vary.It is illustrated below, through 4 steps of generation: one prefilling step (at the top) and 3 decoding steps (below each "Forward pass" lines).

where means "End Of Sequence", this is a special token to indicate the model has reached the end of generation for the corresponding sequence.

The drawback of batched generation is that if one prompt finishes generation before the other one by generating an token, all further generated tokens are useless. And this goes on until the longest request of the batch finishes. Of course, we can remove the prompts that have reached an token from the batch and save some compute and memory, but saving resources is not the goal here: throughput is.

Instead of just removing the finished prompt from the batch, we can replace it with a prompt that's waiting for generation. We will call this dynamic scheduling, or dynamic batching. Dynamic scheduling is great to maintain throughput while ensuring any token generated by a forward pass is relevant. But because of the way we batched prompts together, it has a major drawback: we need a lot of padding when swapping prompts. That's because the newly-inserted prompt needs to go through prefill while the other prompts are decoding one token at a time. So there is almost as much padding as there are tokens in the newly-inserted prompt.

The problem becomes even worse when batch size increases and initial prompts are long. The padding cost grows quadratically with both batch size and prompt length. If we have a batch of B B B prompts that are in decoding phase and one finishes, dynamically introducing a prompt of n n n initial tokens in the batch requires (n−1)(B−1) (n-1)(B-1) (n−1)(B−1) padding tokens. For instance, with B=8 B=8 B=8 and n=100 n=100 n=100, we'd need 99×7=693 99 \times 7 = 693 99×7=693 padding tokens!

According to recent reports, furthermore, practical optimizations like CUDA graphs or torch.compile require static tensor shapes. This forces us to pad all prompts to a fixed maximum length, dramatically increasing the padding waste.

At this point, our main problem is padding, which is a consequence of the axis we added to batch sentences together. Thus, the ideal would be to get rid of this axis entirely, a radical rethinking of batching. If we do so, the only way to batch prompts together is to concatenate them:.

According to recent reports, but we don't want tokens from prompt 0 to interact with the tokens of prompt 1! Luckily for us, we have a way to control how tokens interact with one another: the attention mask. How we do this is displayed below:.

In a recent development, although we use different tints of green to illustrate the different parts of the attention mask, this is still a boolean mask with only greens for True and white for False. This way of batching prompts together is called ragged batching (because sequence lengths are 'ragged' or uneven), and it offers the benefit of added throughput without introducing the need for padding tokens.

In a recent development, in the figure above, we use ragged batching to combine two full prompts together, but we can batch as many as memory allows. The only limit is m m m, the number of tokens we can fit in a batch, with m m m depending on the available memory on the GPU.

Ragged batching is one of the key components of continuous batching. To maximize throughput, we can combine prefill and decoding sequences following an algorithm like this:.

Dynamic scheduling is the final piece that contributes to the continuous batching technique: we remove finished prompts from the batch as soon as they are done, and replace them with new chunked prompts that correspond to incoming requests.

This combination of ragged batching and dynamic scheduling is called continuous batching, and it's the technique that powers modern LLM serving systems.

Continuous batching combines three key techniques to maximize throughput in LLM serving:.

In a recent development, by removing the batch dimension and using attention masks to control token interactions, continuous batching allows mixing prefill and decode phases in the same batch, dramatically improving efficiency for serving multiple requests. This is why services like ChatGPT can handle thousands of concurrent people efficiently.

In a recent development, in the next article in this series, we make continuous batching much more efficient by introducing asynchronous batching. Read it here!If you'd like to see a deep dive on other continuous batching topics, please let us know in the comments!

Thanks for the article! I'd like to add one note: the primary reason we need chunked prefill isn't the memory constraint (otherwise we could simply solve it with Flash Attention). The more practical reason is that a long prefill blocks all decode requests in the batch. Chunking it lets decode requests make progress between chunks. Moreover, since prefill chunks make the forward pass compute-bound, decode tokens can piggyback on the same batch at nearly zero marginal cost - they're just extra rows in an already large matmul. This turns memory-bound decode-only batches into better-utilized compute-saturating ones. See the SARATHI paper for details.

Why Transactional Emails Fail After Deployment: A Practical Debugging Guide for Developers

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transactional emails are easy to overlook during application development. A registration form works, the database stores the user's information, and the backend successfully triggers an email. Everything appears to be functioning as expected.

Then a user reports that their password-reset message never arrived.

It has been revealed that the problem might not be in the email template or the sending function. It could involve DNS configuration, authentication failures, message formatting, queue processing, recipient-server policies, or an incorrectly configured production environment.

For developers building SaaS applications, ecommerce platforms, and web services, reliable email delivery is an crucial part of the user experience. An account-verification message that never arrives can prevent someone from accessing an application, while a delayed security notification can create unnecessary confusion.

Understanding how to investigate these problems requires looking beyond the email-sending function. This guide explores a practical debugging workflow, the technical layers involved, and the tools developers can use to identify common email delivery failures.

One of the first mistakes developers make when troubleshooting email is assuming that a successful API response means the message has reached the recipient.

These are two different events.

When an application submits an email through an SMTP server or an email service provider's API, the provider may accept the request and return a successful response. However, the receiving mail server still needs to process the message.

Depending on its configuration and policies, the receiving server might:.

Accept the message and place it in the inbox.

Accept the message but classify it as spam.

Reject the message because of authentication or policy issues.

Accept the message but place it in another folder.

A successful request therefore confirms only that a particular stage of the process completed.

Developers should distinguish between three crucial states:.

Submission: The application successfully handed the message to its sending provider.

Acceptance: The receiving mail server accepted responsibility for the message.

Inbox placement: The message became visible in the recipient's expected inbox.

These distinctions make troubleshooting considerably easier. Instead of immediately rewriting an email template, developers can identify which stage is actually failing.

Before investigating external email infrastructure, examine the application's own implementation.

According to recent reports, A common example is a password-reset workflow. The application receives a request, generates a temporary token, creates a reset URL, and sends an email containing that URL.

Several problems can occur before the message even reaches an email provider.

The application generates an expired token.

The reset URL points to a staging environment.

An asynchronous task fails before processing the message.

The email service credentials are incorrect.

An API request times out without being retried.

The application records success before confirming the provider's response.

Start by logging the notable stages of the process.

For example, a Node.js application might use structured logging:.

Sources indicate that this example assumes that the email provider returns a message identifier. Adapt the response fields to the actual SDK being used.

Notice that the logs identify the recipient through an internal ID rather than exposing their complete email address.

Avoid logging passwords, authentication tokens, reset URLs, or other sensitive information.

The objective is to establish a traceable record of what happened without introducing additional security risks.

Email authentication is another notable area to investigate when messages are rejected or consistently classified as spam.

Three commonly used mechanisms help receiving servers evaluate whether a message is authorized to represent a particular domain.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allows a domain owner to specify which servers are authorized to send messages using that domain.

This information is published through DNS.

A simplified SPF record might look like this:.

The actual record must reflect the sending services authorized by the domain owner.

Common configuration mistakes include:.

Forgetting to authorize a fresh email provider.

Publishing multiple SPF records for the same domain.

Exceeding SPF's DNS lookup limit.

Leaving outdated sending services in the record.

Recent findings suggest that remember that SPF evaluates the sending infrastructure against the envelope sender domain. It does not automatically guarantee that the visible From address is aligned.

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) adds a cryptographic signature to outgoing messages.

The receiving server can retrieve the corresponding public key through DNS and verify that the signature is valid.

A failed DKIM check might indicate:.

A mismatch between the configured selector and published record.

Message modification after signing.

Developers integrating multiple email providers should verify that each provider has the correct signing configuration.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) builds on SPF and DKIM.

It allows domain owners to define how receiving servers should handle messages that fail authentication and alignment requirements.

A basic monitoring-oriented DMARC record might look like this:.

This is an illustrative configuration. The reporting address must be valid, and the domain should have an appropriate monitoring and policy-enforcement blueprint.

Developers can use MXToolbox to inspect DNS records and investigate common authentication problems.

For additional technical background, SitePoint's guide to HTML email development explains why email environments require different implementation considerations from ordinary web pages.

An email template that looks perfect in a browser can behave differently when rendered by Gmail, Outlook, Apple Mail, or another email client.

This happens because email clients do not implement HTML and CSS in exactly the same way.

A layout may break because of unsupported CSS properties, image restrictions, unexpected font rendering, or differences in how tables are handled.

For this reason, email testing should be part of the development process rather than something performed only after users report a problem.

A useful testing sequence includes:.

HTML validation: Check the markup for malformed elements, missing attributes, and unnecessary code.

Rendering tests: Preview the email across desktop and mobile email clients.

Link verification: Confirm that buttons, links, and personalized URLs point to the correct destinations.

Image testing: Check whether the message remains understandable when images are blocked.

Content inspection: Review subject lines, sender information, and the plain-text alternative.

Deliverability checks: Examine authentication, content-related warnings, and potential inbox placement problems.

Developers can also incorporate pre-send diagnostics into their release workflow to identify potential deliverability problems before a message is sent to a larger audience.

The crucial point is to treat these checks as one part of quality assurance, not as a guarantee that every message will reach the primary inbox.

For more information about email rendering differences, SitePoint's article on essential HTML email coding tips provides useful examples of client-specific behavior.

Testing transactional emails with real customer addresses during development can create unnecessary problems.

A better approach is to use a dedicated testing environment that captures outgoing messages without delivering them to actual recipients.

For example, Mailpit provides a local SMTP server and web interface for inspecting messages during development.

It allows developers to examine:.

Email subject lines and headers.

Embedded images and attachments.

The final output generated by the application.

Another option is Mailtrap, which provides email testing capabilities for development workflows.

Consider a registration feature that sends a welcome message whenever a new user creates an account.

Instead of sending hundreds of test messages to real addresses, developers can configure the development environment to capture them in a testing inbox.

This makes it possible to repeatedly test different templates without affecting actual customers or generating unnecessary email traffic.

A separate testing environment also reduces the risk of accidentally sending development notifications to production customers.

Applications that send large numbers of emails often use background workers instead of processing every message during the original HTTP request.

This approach helps keep the application responsive, but it introduces another potential source of failures.

Imagine an ecommerce application that sends order confirmations after checkout.

The application creates an order successfully and places an email task in a queue. However, the background worker becomes unavailable before processing the task.

The customer receives an order confirmation much later than expected, or perhaps not at all.

To investigate these problems, developers should monitor:.

Retries are particularly important, but they need to be implemented carefully.

A temporary network failure may justify another attempt. A permanent rejection caused by an invalid recipient address usually does not.

Exponential backoff can help prevent repeated requests from overwhelming an unavailable service.

In a production system, add random jitter to avoid having multiple workers retry simultaneously.

In a recent development, also consider idempotency. If a worker processes the same task twice, the application should avoid sending duplicate transactional messages whenever possible.

A reliable queue architecture should distinguish between temporary failures and permanent failures rather than retrying every error indefinitely.

Testing before deployment is important, but it cannot reveal every issue that may occur in production.

Real email traffic introduces changing conditions, including recipient-server behavior, sender reputation, invalid addresses, and differences between email providers.

Developers should therefore establish ongoing monitoring.

For Gmail-related monitoring, Google Postmaster Tools provides information about domain reputation, spam rates, and authentication.

It is particularly useful for teams sending enough email to generate meaningful reporting data.

Another useful resource is Can I Email, which documents HTML and CSS feature support across email clients.

Industry observers note that these tools address different problems. Monitoring sender reputation will not fix a broken password-reset URL, just as validating HTML will not resolve a DNS authentication failure.

The best approach is to monitor each layer independently.

A repeatable checklist helps developers investigate problems without overlooking notable details.

Before releasing a newly introduced email feature, review the following:.

Confirm that the application successfully submits the message.

Verify that provider credentials and environment variables are correct.

Check the SMTP or API response.

Inspect SPF, DKIM, and DMARC configuration.

Validate the HTML and plain-text versions.

Test links and personalized content.

Preview the message on desktop and mobile email clients.

Verify that development and production configurations are separated.

Test queue failures and retry behavior.

Check delivery events and provider error reports.

Monitor bounce and complaint rates after deployment.

Not every application needs an expensive testing platform or a complicated monitoring stack.

A small project might only require a local email testing environment, basic DNS checks, and structured application logs.

A larger SaaS platform may benefit from automated integration tests, provider webhooks, queue monitoring, authentication reports, and dedicated deliverability testing.

The right setup depends on the application's sending volume, complexity, and the importance of its email workflows.

Reliable email delivery requires more than calling an SMTP function or integrating an email API.

Developers need to understand the complete process, from application logic and message construction to authentication, queue processing, recipient-server acceptance, and inbox placement.

The most effective troubleshooting strategy is to isolate these layers instead of treating every missing message as a template problem.

Start with application logs, inspect provider responses, validate authentication records, test email rendering, and monitor production behavior.

By incorporating these checks into development and deployment workflows, teams can reduce avoidable failures and build applications that communicate more reliably with their users.

Diffusers welcomes FLUX-2

📅 25 Nov 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2860 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series.
  • 🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a new image generation and editing model.
  • FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

FLUX.2 is the recent series of image generation models from Black Forest Labs, preceded by the Flux.1 series. It is an entirely latest model with a new architecture and pre-training done from scratch! In this post, we discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2, performing inference with it under various setups, and LoRA fine-tuning.

🚨 FLUX.2 is not meant to be a drop-in replacement of FLUX.1, but a new image generation and editing model.

FLUX.2 can be used for both image-guided and text-guided image generation. Furthermore, it can take multiple images as reference inputs, while producing the final output image. Below, we briefly discuss the key changes introduced in FLUX.2.

First, instead of two text encoders as in Flux.1, it uses a single text encoder — Mistral Small 3.1. Using a single text encoder greatly simplifies the process of computing prompt embeddings. The pipeline allows for a max_sequence_length of 512. Instead of using a single-layer output for the prompt embedding, FLUX.2 stacks outputs from intermediate layers, which have been known to be more beneficial.

Sources indicate that FLUX.2 follows the same general multimodel diffusion transformer (MM-DiT) + parallel DiT architecture as Flux.1. As a refresher, MM-DiT blocks first process the image latents and conditioning text in separate streams, only joining the two together for the attention operation, and are thus referred to as “double-stream” blocks. The parallel blocks then operate on the concatenated image and text streams and can be regarded as “single-stream” blocks.

The key DiT changes from Flux.1 to FLUX.2 are as follows:.

Time and guidance information (in the form of AdaLayerNorm-Zero modulation parameters) is shared across all double-stream and single-stream transformer blocks, respectively, rather than having individual modulation parameters for each block as in Flux.1.

None of the layers in the model use bias parameters. In particular, neither the attention nor feedforward (FF) sub-blocks of either transformer block use bias parameters in any of their layers.

In Flux.1, the single-stream transformer blocks fused the attention output projection with the FF output projection. FLUX.2 single-stream blocks also fuse the attention QKV projections with the FF input projection, creating a fully parallel transformer block:.

Note that compared to the ViT-22B block depicted above, FLUX.2 uses a SwiGLU-style MLP activation rather than a GELU activation (and also doesn’t use bias parameters).

Sources indicate that A larger proportion of the transformer blocks in FLUX.2 are single-stream blocks (8 double-stream blocks to 48 single-stream blocks, compared to 19/38 for Flux.1). This also means that single-stream blocks make up a larger proportion of the DiT parameters: Flux.1[dev]-12B has ~54% of its total parameters in the double-stream blocks, whereas FLUX.2[dev]-32B has ~24% of its parameters in the double-stream blocks (and ~73% in the single-stream blocks).

It has been revealed that FLUX.2 uses a larger DiT and Mistral3 Small as its text encoder. When used together without any kind of offloading, the inference takes more than 80GB VRAM. In the following sections, we show how to perform inference with FLUX.2 in more accessible ways, under various system-level constraints.

Notice that we're using a repository that contains the NF4-quantized versions of the FLUX.2 DiT and the Mistral text encoder.

It has been revealed that due to the modular design of a Diffusers pipeline, we can isolate modules and work with them in sequence. We decouple the text encoder and deploy it to an Inference Endpoint. This helps us with freeing up the VRAM usage for the DiT and VAE only.

You can check out other supported quantization backends here and other memory-saving techniques here.

To check how different quantizations affect an image, you can play with the playground below or access it as standlone in the FLUX.2 Quantization experiments Space.

According to recent reports, FLUX.2 supports using multiple images as inputs, allowing you to use up to 10 images. However, keep in mind that each additional image will require more VRAM. You can reference the images by index (e.g., image 1, image 2) or by natural language (e.g., the kangaroo, the turtle). For optimal results, the best approach is to use a combination of both methods.

It has been revealed that FLUX.2 supports advanced prompting techniques like structured JSON prompting, precise hex color control, and multi-reference image editing. Aside for the added control, this also allows for flexibility in changing specific attributes while maintaining others overall the same.For example, let's start with this json as the base schema (taken from the official FLUX.2 prompting guide):.

Building up on that, let's turn it into a prompt for a shot of a good old fashion walkman on a carpet (simply pass this prompt to your chosen diffusers inference example from above):.

Now, let's change the color of the carpet to a specific teal-blue shade (#367588) and add wired headphones plugged into the walkman:.

The carpet color now matches the hex code provided, and the headphones have been with small changes to the overall scene.

Check out the official prompting guide for more examples and details.

Being both a text-to-image and an image-to-image model, FLUX.2 makes the perfect fine-tuning candidate for many use-cases! However, as inference alone takes more than 80GB of VRAM, LoRA fine-tuning is even more challenging to run on consumer GPUs. To squeeze in as much memory saving as we can, we utilize some of the inference optimizations described above for training as well, together with shared memory saving techniques, to substantially reduce memory consumption. To train it, you can use either the diffusers code below or Ostris' AI Toolkit.

We provide both text-to-image and image-to-image training scripts, for the purpose of this blog will focus on a text-to-image training example.

Recent findings suggest that many of these techniques complement each other and can be used together to reduce memory consumption further. However, some techniques may be mutually exclusive, so be sure to check before launching a training run.

Please make sure to check out the README for prerequisites before starting training.

Recent findings suggest that for this example, we’ll use multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset with the following configuration using FP8 training. Feel free to experiment more with the hyper-parameters and share your results 🤗.

The left image was generated using the pre-trained FLUX.2 model, and the right image was produced the LoRA.

In case your hardware isn’t compatible with FP8 training, you can use QLoRA with bitsandbytes. You first need to define a config.json file like so:.

And then pass its path to --bnb_quantization_config_path:.

What Actually Happens When a Kafka Region Fails?

Sources indicate that most Kafka deployments in the industry plan to survive the loss of a single Kafka broker or an availability zone. But that's not enough for critical Tier-0 infrastructure where downtime or data loss of even a few seconds could have a massive business impact.

In such scenarios, the failure model should consider not just the loss of a broker or a zone, but the loss of an entire region. The business is expected to operate without interruption even when a whole region goes down, and it should be possible to also roll the cluster safely while operating in that state, to apply any break-glass changes.

Industry observers note that but what actually happens inside Kafka when an entire region goes down? What happens to the replicas, producer writes, and KRaft quorum? And what happens when that region comes back?

Let's walk through these scenarios using a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka architecture.

For a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka cluster, we need three different regions with isolated failure domains and a minimum of two brokers in each region.

Brokers in each region should be configured with rack awareness to indicate their failure domains as follows:.

For Tier-0 workloads, each topic's partitions should be configured to have a replication factor (RF) of 6. Kafka's rack-aware replica assignment will spread the replicas across the three regions. If the automatic replica assignment doesn't allocate two replicas per region, we have to explicitly reassign replicas immediately after topic creation to meet our availability guarantees.

This way, if one region goes down entirely, we still have four replicas surviving and the cluster would still continue to operate.

But just running brokers in multiple regions is not the solution here. In fact, that's the easy part. The hard question is, what guarantee remains when one of those regions disappears, and does it solve the business needs?

Let's say Region A goes down entirely.

The two brokers in that region become unavailable, leaving four surviving replicas across Regions B and C.

For any partitions whose leaders were in Region A, Kafka needs to elect upcoming leaders from the surviving in-sync replicas.

But having four surviving replicas alone does not determine whether Kafka will continue accepting writes.

The next step is to define what is considered a successful write in this Kafka setup. For this, we need two configs:.

min.insync.replicas determines the minimum number of replicas that should be present in the in-sync replica set (ISR) of a partition for Kafka to accept writes when producers use acks=all.

acks=all is a producer-side config that ensures that the producer will get an acknowledgment only when the write has been successfully replicated to the required in-sync replicas.

These two settings work together to satisfy the durability guarantees we want.

In a recent development, when all three regions are healthy, ISR would include all six replicas. Let's say one region goes down, then the ISR would drop down to four.

Since minISR is three, writes will still continue to work.

It has been revealed that there may be temporary interruptions while Kafka detects the failure, elects new leaders, and clients reconnect to them. But once the surviving leaders are available, the cluster can continue accepting writes as long as the ISR requirements are met.

The goal isn't availability at any cost, but rather the system should be available as long as the durability guarantees that we designed for can be maintained.

Now let's make the scenario more interesting.

Region A is still down. We have four replicas surviving across Regions B and C.

What if we need to roll the cluster one broker at a time, to apply any break-glass changes?

Recent findings suggest that during that time, the ISR can go down from four to three. But since minISR is three, writes will still continue to work.

Let's look at how the cluster behaves under different failure scenarios.

Kafka will stop accepting writes only when the surviving ISR drops below three.

This is an crucial distinction for Tier-0 workloads.

In a recent development, it's not sufficient to design a cluster that survives a region failure. We also need to consider whether the cluster can continue operating safely while already in that degraded state.

Sources indicate that so far, we focused on the data plane. Now switching gears, the KRaft controllers have a completely different availability model.

They form the metadata quorum, and a majority is needed to continue operation.

For our setup, five controllers could be distributed as 2 + 2 + 1 across the three regions, requiring a majority of three to maintain quorum.

Sources indicate that if either of the regions containing two controllers goes down, three controllers remain. If the region containing one controller goes down, four remain.

So, the controller quorum survives the loss of any one region.

But, unlike brokers, we cannot necessarily roll the controllers at that point because taking one controller down could cause the quorum to drop below three.

According to recent reports, with a static quorum, one way to solve this is to use more controllers, and a 3 + 3 + 3 distribution would provide this. Losing one region would leave six controllers with room to still roll the controllers, as we only need five to maintain quorum.

On the flip side, an increase in quorum size also increases the coordination overhead. The official Kafka documentation typically recommends three or five controllers, which tolerate one or two concurrent failures respectively.

Alternatively, with dynamic KRaft quorum (KIP-853), introduced in Kafka 3.9, we can add or remove controllers from the voting quorum without restarting the cluster.

For example, with our 2 + 2 + 1 setup, if a region containing two controllers goes down, the remaining three controllers can still maintain quorum. We can then remove the failed controllers from the voting membership, one at a time, reducing the quorum size to three. This allows us to roll one of the surviving controllers while still maintaining the fresh majority of two.

Recent findings suggest that however, dynamic quorum reconfiguration is not automatic. The surviving controllers must be able to maintain quorum and successfully commit the membership changes before we can proceed with the controller restart.

You need to consider whether you want the same availability guarantee for the controllers as that of the data plane, and whether dynamic quorum reconfiguration during a regional outage is acceptable for your Tier-0 workloads.

So far, we assumed that a region either works or goes down completely.

But the WAN itself becomes a failure mode.

In this setup, a partly working WAN between two regions can be more dangerous than a link that's completely down.

Increased latency, packet loss, or intermittent connectivity issues between regions can cause replication to lag, ultimately resulting in replicas falling out of ISR.

The three regions might be independently healthy, but if the connectivity between them is not, then the availability of the cluster might be impacted.

Going back to the CAP theorem, to tolerate a network partition, we must choose between consistency and availability.

So, if a partition's ISR falls below the configured min.insync.replicas of three due to a network partition, Kafka stops accepting writes with acks=all rather than weakening those guarantees.

Similarly, if the KRaft controller quorum is lost, then no metadata changes, like leader elections, can happen in the cluster, even though existing data-plane traffic may continue for some time.

The availability guarantees we discussed also come with their own costs.

The first cost is client latency. With cross-region replication and acks=all, the network latency between these regions directly affects producer latency. Consumers can also pay the WAN latency cost when consuming from partition leaders located in a different region.

The second cost is replication overhead. With RF=6, there is additional storage, network traffic, and replication-related coordination cost in the brokers compared to a smaller number of replicas.

So, in an architecture like this, monitoring the health of the network paths between these regions is as critical as monitoring the Kafka brokers and controllers.

Metrics like round-trip latency (RTT) between regions, packet loss, TCP retransmissions, connection errors/timeouts, and network throughput/bandwidth utilization are a good start.

When one region goes down, all the partition leaders in that region would move to the two other surviving regions.

This implies that those two regions would have to handle more producer and consumer traffic, network throughput, and disk I/O.

Even if the cluster is designed to satisfy its ISR and controller quorum requirements, if it's not sized to handle these failures when one region goes down, the surviving regions would be overloaded, resulting in higher latencies, timeouts, and operational instability.

So, for Tier-0 infrastructure, capacity planning should always be done for failure states and not stop at normal operations.

Now let's say Region A comes back online.

The brokers in the recovered region might have to catch up on a significant amount of data before they become fully in sync again.

This can result in a sudden burst of cross-region network traffic and disk I/O across all regions.

Region recovery needs to be controlled so that it doesn't overwhelm the healthy part of the cluster.

This can be achieved by throttling the replica catch-up, with the trade-off of longer recovery time to minimize the impact on live production traffic.

Replication throttling needs a deeper discussion of its own, so we won't go into details here.

Recent findings suggest that the vital point is that bringing a failed region back online is not simply a matter of restarting its brokers. We need to make sure that the recovery process itself doesn't impact the business.

Before putting a Tier-0 multi-region Kafka cluster into production, validate these scenarios:.

Recent findings suggest that there is no shortage of ways to deploy Kafka across multiple regions. The challenge here is to pick the right architecture that addresses all our durability guarantees.

For Tier-0 workloads, this means designing the architecture around failures first.

Sources indicate that what happens when a region goes down? Can we still roll the cluster? What continues to work, and at what point do we deliberately stop accepting writes?

Lastly, can we safely bring back the region that was down without impacting the business?

That is ultimately the difference between simply running Kafka across multiple regions versus actually supporting a mission-critical Tier-0 workload.

#35001. Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2024 w)

Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020.
  • Today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯.
  • The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020. Five years later, we now release v5.0.0rc-0.

Today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯. Altogether, it has now surpassed 1.2 billion installs!

The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.

This growth is powered by the evolution of the field and the now mainstream access to AI. As a leading model-definition library in the ecosystem, we need to continuously evolve and adapt the library to continue being relevant. Reinvention is key for longevity in AI.

We’re fortunate to collaborate with many libraries and apps built on transformers, in no specific order: llama.cpp, MLX, onnxruntime, Jan, LMStudio, vLLM, SGLang, Unsloth, LlamaFactory, dLLM, MaxText, TensorRT, Argmax, among many other friends.

Sources indicate that for v5, we wanted to work on several notable aspects: simplicity, training, inference, and production. We detail the work that went into them in this post.

The first focus of the team was on simplicity. Working on transformers, we see the code as the product. We want our model integrations to be clean, so that the ecosystem may depend on our model definitions and understand what’s really happening under the hood, how models differ from each other, and the key features of each newly introduced model. Simplicity results in wider standardization, generality, and wider support.

Recent findings suggest that transformers is the backbone of hundreds of thousands of projects, Unsloth included. We build on Transformers to help people fine-tune and train models efficiently, whether that’s BERT, text-to-speech (TTS), or others; to run fast inference for reinforcement learning (RL) even when models aren’t yet supported in other libraries. We're excited for Transformers v5 and are super happy to be working with the Hugging Face team!

Transformers, at the core, remains a model architecture toolkit. We aim to have all recent architectures and to be the “source of truth” for model definitions. We’ve been adding between 1 - 3 newly introduced models every week for 5 years, shown in the timeline below:.

We’ve worked on improving that model-addition process.

Over the past year, we’ve heavily pushed our modular design as a significant step forward. This allows for easier maintenance, faster integration, and better collaboration across the community.

Sources indicate that we give a deeper overview in our Maintain the Unmaintainable blog post. For brevity, we aim to achieve a much easier model contribution process, as well as a lower maintenance burden. One metric we can highlight is that the number of lines of code to contribute (and review), drop significantly when modular is used:.

It has been revealed that while we respect the “One model, one file” philosophy, we continue introducing some abstractions making the management of common helpers simpler. The prime example of this is the introduction of the AttentionInterface, which offers a centralized abstraction for attention methods. The eager method will remain in the modeling file; others, such as FA1/2/3, FlexAttention, or SDPA, are moved to the interface.

Over the past couple of years, the increasing amount of 0-day support for upcoming model architectures and standardization of attention handling has helped to simplify our support for post-training modern LLMs.

In a recent development, we’re building tooling to help us identify which existing model architecture a newly introduced model resembles. This feature uses machine learning to find code similarities between independent modeling files. Going further, we aim to automate the conversion process by opening a draft PR for the model to be integrated into our transformers format. This process reduces manual effort and ensures consistency.

We’ve significantly refactored the modeling and tokenization files. Modeling files have been greatly improved thanks to the modular approach mentioned above, on top of standardization across models. Standardization contributes to abstracting most of the tools that don’t make up a model, so that the modeling code only contains the relevant parts for a model’s forward/backward passes.

Alongside this work, we’re simplifying the tokenization and processing files: going forward, we’ll only focus on the tokenizers backend, removing the concept of “Fast” and “Slow” tokenizers.

We'll use tokenizers as our main tokenization backend, just as we do for PyTorch-based models. We’ll offer alternatives for Sentencepiece or MistralCommon backed tokenizers, which will be non-default but will be supported. Image processors will now only exist with their fast variant, which depends on the torchvision backend.

Finally, we’re sunsetting our Flax/TensorFlow support in favor of focusing on PyTorch as the sole backend; however, we're also working with partners in the Jax ecosystem to ensure we have compatibility between our models and this ecosystem.

In a recent development, with its v5 release, transformers is going all in on PyTorch. Transformers acts as a source of truth and foundation for modeling across the field; we've been working with the team to ensure good performance across the stack.

We're excited to continue pushing for this in the future across training, inference, and deployment.

-- Matt White, Executive Director, PyTorch Foundation. GM of AI, Linux Foundation.

Training remains a substantial focus of the team as we head into v5: whereas previously we would focus heavily on fine-tuning rather than pre-training/full-training at scale, we’ve recently done significant work to improve our support for the latter as well.

Supporting pre-training meant reworking the initialization of our models, ensuring that they worked at scale with different parallelism paradigms, and shipping support for optimized kernels for both the forward and backward passes.

Going forward, we’re excited to have extended compatibility with torchtitan, megatron, nanotron, as well as any other pre-training tool that is interested in collaborating with us.

We continue collaborating closely with all fine-tuning tools in the Python ecosystem. We aim to continue providing model implementations compatible with Unsloth, Axolotl, LlamaFactory, TRL and others in the PyTorch ecosystem; but we are also working with tools such as MaxText, in the JAX ecosystem, to have good interoperability between their frameworks and transformers.

All fine-tuning and post-training tools can now rely on transformers for model definitions; further enabling Agentic use-cases through OpenEnv or the Prime Environment Hub.

We’re putting a significant focus on inference for v5, with several paradigm changes: the introduction of specialized kernels, cleaner defaults, upcoming APIs, support for optimized inference engines.

Similarly to training, we’ve been putting some effort in packaging kernels so that they’re automatically used in case your hardware and software permits it. If you haven’t heard of kernels before, we recommend taking a look at this doc.

Alongside this effort, we ship two new APIs dedicated to inference:.

Sources indicate that we see this as a major step forward for use-cases such as evaluation, where a great number of inference requests are done simultaneously. We don’t aim to do specialized optimizations like the dedicated inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT LLM). Instead, we aim to be perfectly inter-compatible with these, as detailed in the next section.

In a recent development, the Transformers backend in vLLM has been very enabling to get more architectures, like BERT and other encoders, available to more users. We've been working with the Transformers team to ensure many models are available across modalities with the best performance possible. This is just the start of our collaboration: we're happy to see the Transformers team will have this as a focus going into version 5.

-- Simon Mo, Harry Mellor at vLLM.

In a recent development, standardization is key to accelerating AI innovation. Transformers v5 empowers the SGLang team to spend less time on model reimplementation and more time on kernel optimization. We look forward to building a more efficient and unified AI ecosystem together!

Recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

Industry observers note that we've also been working very closely with ONNXRuntime, llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

The Transformers framework is the go-to place for reference AI model implementations. The framework plays a crucial role in enabling modern AI across the entire stack. The team and the community behind the project truly understand and embrace the spirit of the open-source development and collaboration.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

According to recent reports, it’s hard to overstate the importance of Transformers (and datasets, tokenizers, etc) to the open-source and overall AI ecosystem. I can’t count the number of times I’ve personally used Transformers as a source-of-truth.

According to recent reports, finally, we’re pushing the boundaries of local inference and are working hand-in-hand with the executorch team to get the transformers models to be available on-device. We’re expanding the coverage to multimodal models (vision, audio) through optimum.

Quantization is quickly emerging as the standard for state-of-the-art model development. Many SOTA models are now released in low-precision formats such as 8-bit and 4-bit (e.g., gpt-oss, Kimi-K2, Deepseek-r1), hardware is increasingly optimized for low-precision workloads, and the community is actively sharing high-quality quantized checkpoints. In v5, we're making quantization a central focus of Transformers support, ensuring full compatibility with all major features, and delivering a reliable framework for training and inference.

We introduce a significant change to the way we load weights in our models; and with this, we move to quantization being a first-class citizen.

Our collaboration with the Transformers team was highly productive, marked by their proactive code reviews, feedback, and technical expertise. Their support was crucial in integrating TorchAO, expanding quantization features, and improving documentation for broader adoption in the V5.

According to recent reports, we're excited that v5 has made quantization a first-class citizen. It provides the foundation for bitsandbytes to better support key features like TP and MoEs, and also makes it easier to integrate latest quantization methods.

-- Matthew Douglas & Titus von Koeller, bitsandbytes.

Industry observers note that the overarching theme of this version 5 release is “interoperability”. All refactors, performance improvements, and standardization are aligned with this theme. v5 plays nicely and end-to-end with the growing ecosystem: train a model with Unsloth/Axolotl/LlamaFactory/MaxText deploy it with vLLM/SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp/executorch/MLX to run locally!

Version 5 is undeniably an accomplishment of the past five years by a very large number of people in our community. We also see it as a promise, and as a beacon of the direction we want to go.

It has been revealed that we took it as an opportunity to clean up the toolkit and isolate what mattered; we now have a clean slate on top of which to build. Thanks to the many changes from the community and team, improvements in performance, usability, and readability, will be simpler to ship.

It has been revealed that now that v5.0.0's first RC is out there, we'll be eagerly awaiting your feedback. Please check our release notes for all the technical details, and we'll be awaiting your feedback in our GitHub issues!

We Got Claude to Fine-Tune an Open Source LLM

📅 04 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a latest tool called Hugging Face Skills.
  • According to recent reports, claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks.
  • Sources indicate that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a latest tool called Hugging Face Skills. Not just write training scripts, but to actually submit jobs to cloud GPUs, monitor progress, and push finished models to the Hugging Face Hub. This tutorial shows you how it works and how to use it yourself.

According to recent reports, claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks. The hf-llm-trainer skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about training: which GPU to pick for your model size, how to configure Hub authentication, when to use LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and how to handle the dozens of other decisions that go into a successful training run.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

Sources indicate that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

It has been revealed that this isn't a toy demo. The skill supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 70B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

In a recent development, hugging Face skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. With integrations on the way for Cursor, Windsurf, and Continue.

This repo includes gemini-extension.json to integrate with the Gemini CLI.

You have to authenticate to your Hugging Face account with a write-access token so that the job can create a model repo.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use your write token by sending it in either the HF_TOKEN or Authorization: Bearer HTTP Headers.

For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hf-skills https://huggingface.co/mcp?bouquet=skills --header "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN".

In a recent development, let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to see the full workflow, then explore more advanced capabilities.

Start with a simple and clear instruction to fine tune a specific model.

Sources indicate that the coding agent analyzes your request and prepares a training configuration. For a 0.6B model on a demo dataset, it selects t4-small—enough GPU for this model size and the cheapest option available.

Recent findings suggest that the open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

Recent findings suggest that this works for vision language models too! You can simply run "Fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on llava-instruct-mix".

Before your coding agent submits anything, you'll see the configuration:.

Sources indicate that this is your chance to adjust anything. Change the output repo name, pick different hardware, or ask Claude to modify training parameters. Once you approve, the agent submits the job.

For example, you can ask the agent to try a test run:.

After submission, you get job details:.

The skill includes Trackio integration, so you can watch training loss decrease in real-time. Jobs run asynchronously so you can close your terminal and come back later. When you want an upgrade:.

Then the agent fetches the logs and summarizes progress.

When training completes, your model is on the Hub:.

That's the full loop. You described what you wanted in plain English, and the agent handled GPU selection, script generation, job submission, authentication, and persistence. The whole thing cost about thirty cents.

Industry observers note that the skill supports three training approaches. Understanding when to use each one helps you get better results.

Recent findings suggest that SFT is where most projects start. You provide demonstration data—examples of inputs and desired outputs—and training adjusts the model to match those patterns.

Use SFT when you have high-quality examples of the behavior you want. Customer support conversations, code generation pairs, domain-specific Q&A—anything where you can show the model what good looks like.

The agent validates the dataset, selects hardware (a10g-large with LoRA for a 7B model), and configures training with checkpoints and monitoring.

Sources indicate that for models larger than 3B parameters, the agent automatically uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce memory requirements. This makes training 7B or 13B models feasible on single GPUs while preserving most of the quality of full fine-tuning.

DPO trains on preference pairs—responses where one is "chosen" and another is "rejected." This aligns model outputs with human preferences, typically after an initial SFT stage.

In a recent development, use DPO when you have preference annotations from human labelers or automated comparisons. DPO optimizes directly for the preferred response without needing a separate reward model.

Sources indicate that DPO is sensitive to dataset format. It requires columns named exactly chosen and rejected, or a prompt column with the input. The agent validates this first and shows you how to map columns if your dataset uses different names.

In a recent development, you can run DPO using Skills on vision language models too! Try it out with openbmb/RLAIF-V-Dataset. Claude will apply minor modifications but will succeed in training.

GRPO is a reinforcement learning task that is proven to be effective on verifiable tasks like solving math problems, writing code, or any task with a programmatic success criterion.

The model generates responses, receives rewards based on correctness, and learns from the outcomes. This is more complex than SFT or DPO, but the configuration is similar.

The agent selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions.

For tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train quickly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

It has been revealed that for small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

For medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable.

When testing a workflow, start small:.

The coding agent configures minimal training—enough to verify your pipeline works without real cost.

Recent findings suggest that always run a demo before committing to a multi-hour production job. A $0.50 demo that catches a format error saves a $30 failed run.

Dataset format is the most common source of training failures. The agent can validate datasets before you spend GPU time.

The agent runs a quick inspection on CPU (fractions of a penny) and reports:.

If your dataset needs transformation, the agent can show you how:.

The agent provides mapping code and can incorporate it directly into your training script.

It has been revealed that real-time monitoring helps you catch problems early. The skill configures Trackio by default—after submitting a job, you can watch metrics at:.

Industry observers note that this shows training loss, learning rate, and validation metrics. A healthy run shows steadily decreasing loss.

Ask the agent about status anytime:.

If something goes wrong, the agent helps diagnose. Out of memory? the agent suggests reducing batch size or upgrading hardware. Dataset error? The agent identifies the mismatch. Timeout? The agent recommends longer duration or faster training settings.

It has been revealed that after training, you might want to run your model locally. The GGUF format works with llama.cpp and dependent tools like LM Studio, Ollama, etc.

The agent submits a conversion job that merges LoRA adapters, converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to Hub.

We've shown that coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI can handle the full lifecycle of model fine-tuning: validating data, selecting hardware, generating scripts, submitting jobs, monitoring progress, and converting outputs. This turns what used to be a specialized skill into something you can do through conversation.

The skill is open source. You can extend it, customize it for your workflows, or use it as a starting point for other training scenarios.
